We therefore treat issue-driven testing as a distinct setting for environment construction and experience collection. A repository supplies the application, and its issue report specifies behavior that browser interaction can test.

Figure 17 shows how browser testing guides successive code revisions. We first prepare a runnable project and turn the issue into a fixed test expectation. A coding agent then revises and launches the application, making a candidate repair available to the web agent. The web agent replays the reported interactions and compares their effects with the expectation. Finally, its action trace, screenshots, and verdict return to the coding agent in a test report. This evidence directs the next repair while keeping every iteration focused on the same issue.

Environment preparation begins with GitHub frontend repositories whose issues describe browser-reproducible behavior. The builder installs dependencies, starts the project, and prepares the pages and data involved in the issue. This makes the reported problem available for direct interaction and supplies the workspace in which repairs will be tested.

The issue then defines what to check in this workspace. Its expected behavior supplies the coding agent’s repair objective and a test list of browser actions and expected results for the web agent. For example, an issue may report that an edited page title appears to save but disappears after reload. The corresponding test changes the title, saves it, reloads the page, and checks that the new title remains. Both the code change and its assessment therefore address the same user-reported problem.

The coding agent inspects the relevant implementation using the issue and any feedback from the previous browser test. It then changes the code and launches the revised application. These actions, illustrated by the editor views in Figure 17(2), supply a runnable candidate whose behavior still needs to be tested.

The web agent performs the test actions against that candidate and captures the resulting states. A visible save confirmation establishes what the interface showed immediately after saving. Reloading tests whether the change persists. In the illustrated failure, the edited title appears after save but the old title returns after reload.

The browser test report links these states to the actions that produced them and states the discrepancy directly. The stacked views in Figure 17(3) follow the same R17 record through editing, saving, and reloading. Because the edited title should persist, the observed old title identifies a discrepancy for the coding agent to investigate. This feedback guides its next revision, which the web agent tests again through the running interface. The issue’s expected behavior remains fixed across iterations. This loop supplies GUI interaction trajectories and outcome feedback tied to real development requests, with evidence qualification and final acceptance detailed in Appendix F.1.

Case study of a responsive homepage repair.

Figure 18 follows a local Mercedes-Benz GLE SUV homepage built from supplied materials. The request called for a responsive page with usable controls and navigation. Two defects emerged when the WebTestAgent followed a button click over time and inspected the page at a narrow width.

In the first browser test (R1), the WebTestAgent clicked Learn more and waited. The transient notification disappeared, leaving no stable confirmation. Resizing the page to 320 px then exposed a second defect, with text navigation covering the centered logo. The R1 report on the left links both findings to the actions and screenshots that exposed them, giving the Coding Agent two specific behaviors to repair.

The central patch excerpts show how this feedback changed the code. For the first finding, the Coding Agent added an HTML confirmation element below the button and updated its text through the JavaScript click handler, so the response could remain visible. For the second, a CSS rule hid the text links at widths up to 560 px while retaining the hamburger menu. This freed space around the logo while preserving navigation access. The matching numbers connect each reported defect to its corresponding patch.

With the revised page running, the Coding Agent requested a second browser test (R2). The WebTestAgent clicked the button again, waited three seconds, and changed the carousel slide. The inline confirmation remained visible. At 320 px, the links no longer covered the logo, the menu opened and closed, and the page had no horizontal overflow. Together with a homepage visual check, these observations supported PASS on three selected items from R1’s five-item checklist. The two reported defects were resolved in this targeted retest.

Together, these routes expand environment supply from user requests, reference websites, and runnable software projects. Their prepared workspaces support experience collection, and reconstructed sites also feed new task generation through Scaling Intents. Tasks equipped with reliable executable verifiers offer a further route to expansion: the next section uses their goals and outcome checks as seeds for additional task construction.

4.2.3  Scaling Verifiers

Task datasets and manually authored cases provide user goals already paired with executable verifiers. A reliable verifier makes the intended outcome explicit and supplies a repeatable check on collected trajectories. Creating additional checks is costly, however, because each needs to match its task and distinguish correct results from plausible mistakes. We design Scaling Verifiers to expand this resource by adapting existing task–verifier pairs (Wang et al., 2026a; Lv et al., 2026).

Figure 19 illustrates the construction and validation phases. We first use a seed’s goal and success conditions to construct related tasks, changing the request, initial state, and verifier together. The new pair then undergoes a GUI execution trial and tests of the verifier’s judgments. Their findings guide repairs before the pair enters collection.

This joint treatment matters because changing a request’s selection criterion also changes which records the verifier should accept as updated and which it should require to remain intact.

Expanding the work and its success conditions.

The construction agent reads the seed request, initialization, and verifier to identify useful subgoals, their prerequisites, and the observable changes that establish success. A subgoal can involve several GUI actions, such as editing a document and exporting the result. We use these subgoals in three different ways. Decomposition extracts a meaningful part of the seed task. Variation changes the condition or operation while retaining its basic structure. Composition connects subgoals into a longer workflow, whose later work uses earlier results. The approval example in Figure 19 shows the effect of each choice on the requested work and the corresponding outcome checks.

  • •

    Decomposition turns a meaningful part of the workflow into a task of its own. Extracting record selection yields a request to identify the qualifying records, an initial state containing the required data, and a verifier for the returned selection and preservation of all records.

  • •

    Variation changes the materials, parameters, or operations. A new selection criterion leads to a new target set derived from the corresponding input records. The request and verifier are updated to express and assess that change.

  • •

    Composition joins compatible subgoals through their inputs and outputs. Adding a summary export to an approval task makes the approved identifiers the contents of the later file. The adapted verifier checks the updates, the exported summary, and preservation of the records the request protects. The added dependency can produce a more demanding multi-stage task.

Across these changes, the agent resolves the actual identifiers and file references used by the request, environment, and verifier. In the composition example, the targets established during selection remain the targets during assessment, even when the update changes a field used for selection. Desktop compositions carry the same relationship through documents and intermediate files. Requirements that matter during a stage are checked there, while final-state requirements are assessed at completion.

Testing the task and its verifier.

Each rewritten task undergoes two complementary checks before collection. A GUI trial examines whether an agent can carry out the request from the prepared state. Verifier probes examine whether the checker judges known outcomes as the task requires. The lower part of Figure 19 keeps these two sources of evidence separate.

For the execution trial, we run a CUA from the declared initial state with the rewritten request. Its interaction and resulting state reveal problems such as missing inputs, unreachable controls, or instructions inconsistent with the workspace. These findings identify which setup or request needs repair.

To test the verifier itself, we construct outcome probes whose expected verdicts follow from the request and starting data, then compare those verdicts with the verifier’s outputs. In the approval-and-export example, a complete result should pass, whereas an otherwise correct update without the required export should fail. Additional probes isolate incomplete updates, changes to protected records, and allowed alternative outputs. A disagreement identifies a checker rule to revise, even when the GUI task itself can be completed.

We collect trial failures and verifier disagreements into a construction report. Setup and instruction failures return to task construction, while incorrect verdicts return to the verifier. After the revision, we rerun the affected tests against the same intended requirements before admitting the pair to collection. Requirements that need contextual judgment use the evaluator in Section 3.3. This feedback loop keeps task expansion connected to executable conditions and meaningful outcome assessment.

The three construction routes supply tasks to the shared collection service (Section 3.4). Executing these tasks produces trajectories and outcome assessments. Obtaining successful experience from the hardest tasks introduces the next challenge.

4.3  Recursive Self-Improvement for Hard-Task Collection

The routes in Section 4.2 supply executable tasks whose rollouts provide experience for learning. During collection, however, we encounter long and difficult tasks that remain unsolved within the ordinary budget. Collecting demonstrations of sustained planning and recovery from these tasks requires addressing two recurring obstacles. Repeated attempts can lose useful discoveries and repeat ineffective procedures. A late failure can also force a new attempt to rebuild substantial earlier work.

We design two recursive self-improvement (RSI) pipelines for collecting experience from these tasks. Each carries forward the information needed to address one of these obstacles.

  • •

    Knowledge accumulation. Skill-guided recursive exploration turns trial-and-error findings into tested procedures that guide subsequent attempts (Figure 20).

  • •

    Progress accumulation. Milestone-guided trajectory search preserves completed work and resumes exploration from the corresponding software state and agent context (Figure 21).

Both use feedback from earlier trials to shape later exploration (Zhu et al., 2026). They target tasks that pass construction checks but remain unsuccessful in ordinary collection. The original acceptance conditions stay fixed. We check the completed task before admitting an assisted trajectory as a full-task demonstration. Milestone-guided collection can also retain verified subtask traces from attempts that leave the full task unfinished.

4.3.1  Skill-Guided Recursive Exploration

Some GUI tasks require a procedure that the agent has not discovered. The difficulty may be an unfamiliar application command, a hidden prerequisite, or a sequence whose useful effect becomes clear only after trying it and inspecting the result. Repeated attempts can make partial discoveries, but those discoveries remain scattered across their histories unless the collector carries them forward. We therefore need a way to turn trial-and-error experience into reusable operating guidance.

We design a skill-guided loop with four stages, shown in Figure 20. Task-directed exploration first produces observations about useful operations and unresolved obstacles. A skill creator then reviews that experience and consolidates actionable findings into written guidance. A separate agent tests the candidate instructions before they are supplied to a new task attempt. That attempt can use the validated procedure to make further progress, and its new discoveries feed the next round of skill refinement. The loop accumulates tested knowledge across attempts while retaining full-task verification for the final result.

Explore the task and identify obstacles.

We use a computer-use agent to attempt the original query in its prepared workspace. It inspects the relevant applications and files, tries controls, and adjusts its action sequence as it observes their effects. An unsuccessful attempt can still reveal an important prerequisite, an ineffective action to avoid, or a way to reach a previously inaccessible state. Successful operations likewise show procedures worth retaining. We examine these findings in the trajectory and result, using evaluator observations of the live state to help identify the remaining obstacle (Section 3.3) (Shinn et al., 2023).

In the representative report workflow in Figure 20, exploration may reveal several export options. One trial produces a PDF with all the required pages but represents their text as an image. The searchability check then focuses further trials on which export settings preserve text. The initial exploration has thus turned a broad completion goal into a specific procedural question that can be tested in the application.

Consolidate a candidate skill.

The skill creator reviews the accumulated trajectories and their outcomes. When the useful procedure is still unclear, further exploration or focused practice tests alternative operations. The creator turns the resulting findings into textual guidance that states when the procedure applies, which actions to take, and how to check its intended effect (Wang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026c). For the PDF example, this means recording the text-preserving export settings and a search check, together with the image-only choice to avoid. The candidate gives later attempts a concrete procedure and the relevant pitfall.

Validate the skill independently.

Guidance inferred from exploratory trials may omit a prerequisite or misidentify why an operation worked. We therefore freeze the candidate and give it to a separate agent in an independent validation trial. The agent applies the instructions and checks their claimed effect in the environment.

In the PDF example, it exports using the specified settings and searches for a phrase from the source document. Finding the phrase establishes the intended effect of this skill, while a failed check returns the instructions to exploration and revision. The revised candidate is tested again before admission for reuse.

Reuse the skill and continue exploration.

We provide the validated guidance to a new attempt at the original task. The agent can now use the tested procedure when it reaches the relevant operation. If it encounters another obstacle, or discovers a useful way to complete a later stage, that experience feeds the same consolidation and validation loop. Previously validated skills remain available, so each round can build on what earlier attempts established.

The process continues until an attempt satisfies the original task’s full acceptance conditions or the exploration budget is exhausted. Accepted attempts supply trajectories with the actual guidance retained in their decision context. The skill library also makes a tested procedure available to later tasks that meet its applicability conditions. This accumulation is designed to improve hard-task collection by carrying useful knowledge between attempts. The TERRA dashboard case in Section 4.3.3 follows how a charting problem becomes revised guidance that a fresh attempt applies (Figure 22).

For a long workflow, however, even a better-informed attempt can spend substantial effort repeating earlier work. The next pipeline addresses that remaining cost by retaining execution progress.

4.3.2  Milestone-Guided Trajectory Search

A long task can be difficult to finish in a single attempt even when its individual stages are within the agent’s reach. When a late failure ends an attempt, restarting from the initial state repeats work already completed. This motivates a second RSI strategy in which collection focuses on smaller, verifiable goals and retains the work that reaches them.

We design milestone-guided trajectory search to implement this strategy. We first decompose the original task into dependent milestones and their checks. GUI attempts then work toward one milestone at a time, saving the workspace and agent context when a check passes. Further attempts restore that checkpoint to explore the next stage, following the principle of returning to useful states for exploration (Ecoffet et al., 2021). After the final milestone, the original verifier checks the complete result before the selected path becomes a full-task demonstration. Figure 21 illustrates how this process builds successful continuations on retained progress. It reduces the work each trial needs to repeat while keeping acceptance tied to the original task. A construction case in Section 4.3.3 follows this accumulation of progress from an empty Blender scene to a complete collected trajectory (Figure 23).

Define milestones and their checks.

We use a planning agent to read the user request and the original verifier code, identify dependencies, and propose meaningful intermediate goals. Each milestone pairs a subtask with a check on its observable result. The goal should represent useful progress and leave a state from which later work can continue. Reviewing the pairs against the original requirements ensures that local checks support the intended full task. This uses the decomposition principle in Section 4.2.3, here to guide collection within one long task.

For the office workflow in Figure 21, the original goal includes updating a business record and producing a searchable PDF. We organize it into three milestones: complete the record update (M1), prepare the report (M2), and export the searchable PDF (M3). Their checks inspect the corresponding records, document content, and output file. The executing agent receives the permitted subtask guidance, while private verifier constants remain in the checking context.

Preserve progress and explore continuations.

The harness supplies the first subtask to a computer-use agent in the initial workspace and runs repeated attempts within the collection budget. When an attempt passes the milestone check, we save an E2B workspace snapshot together with the agent context about completed work, useful findings, and remaining goals. Restoring both gives the next attempt a consistent starting point for the following milestone (Section 3.2). We retain the full interaction prefix alongside the bounded decision context and can keep several passing states to support different continuations.

Retained checkpoints form the nodes of a search tree, and GUI action sequences toward the next milestone form its branches. Each continuation restores its parent checkpoint in an isolated instance, observes the interface, and attempts the next stage. Passing results become checkpoints for the next milestone. If a continuation stalls or fails its check, its parent remains available so that a new attempt can try a different sequence without replaying the earlier stages.

We can also retain selected recoverable failed states for further exploration. These states keep their unresolved milestone labels. A continuation attempts the necessary correction before advancing to later goals, allowing the collected path to include genuine recovery from an earlier mistake. Thus the tree can support both alternative attempts from verified progress and recovery attempts from a useful but incomplete state.

In Figure 21, branches A and C fail the export requirement, while B produces a searchable PDF. All three begin at M2, retaining the same earlier record update and report preparation. A failed export can also trigger the skill exploration described above, whose validated guidance can be used by a new continuation. The saved checkpoint preserves the work already done, and the skill helps the agent choose how to perform the unresolved operation.

Verify outcomes and retain useful traces.

After the final milestone, the original task verifier assesses candidate completions against all requirements, including those established in earlier stages. For the office task, it checks the PDF, the required record update, and source preservation. Search continues until a branch passes this final check or the budget is exhausted. A passing branch yields a search-assisted trajectory: the actual parent–child path from the initial state to completion, combining its retained prefix with the selected continuations. It keeps the path’s observations, actions, and supplied guidance, including mistakes followed by recovery. Failed sibling branches remain exploration records and are not spliced into the accepted trajectory.

If an attempt completes only part of the milestone sequence, we retain only the trace portions associated with passed milestones as subtask-level demonstrations, preserving their original decision context. This recovers useful supervision from unfinished attempts and makes fuller use of the collection budget.

4.3.3  Case Studies of Knowledge and Progress Accumulation

We use two case studies to explain how the RSI strategies collect experience on difficult tasks. The first follows skill refinement while building a live retail dashboard in Calc. The second follows milestone accumulation while constructing a greenhouse cafe in Blender. In each case, the recorded attempts show what goes wrong and how retaining knowledge or progress helps subsequent attempts complete the task.

Knowledge accumulation in a dashboard task.

Figure 22 starts with a request to build a quarterly operations dashboard for TERRA from sales records and store targets. The deliverables are an editable workbook with live calculations and charts, and a matching one-page PDF. The request specifies grouped vertical columns and a navy, teal, and orange palette. The difficulty is translating these visual requirements into Calc’s orientation and color settings, whose effects need to be checked in the saved workbook and exported PDF.

In Attempt 1, the agent follows skill v1, which asks for grouped columns and final document inspection. These instructions leave the relevant API settings unspecified. The agent sets Vertical=True through the legacy chart interface, producing the horizontal bars shown in the top row. It discovers the correct setting and fixes the direction during this attempt, but the charts retain the default blue and red series colors. The final palette check therefore rejects the delivery.

Reviewing this trajectory identifies the two changes shown in the middle of the figure. Skill v2 records Vertical=False as the setting for vertical columns and adds explicit series-color assignment through chart2, followed by property readback and visual inspection. Engineering probes check these procedures before the revised skill is fixed in a new attempt’s context. Attempt 2 then starts from the original input in a fresh workspace. It applies the orientation setting and assigns teal to net sales and orange to the target series before exporting the dashboard. The bottom row shows the resulting columns, palette, and PDF. The completed task passes all 26 final checks, including input-change tests of the live formulas and charts. Earlier trial-and-error has thus become precise operating guidance that the next attempt can apply to produce a verified demonstration.

Progress accumulation in a 3D modeling task.

Figure 23 follows a request to build ORBIT BOTANICA, a futuristic greenhouse cafe, from an empty Blender scene and deliver an editable model with its final render. The task combines structural, equipment, and appearance requirements, so an error in the final render can arise after much of the construction is complete.

We apply the milestone-guided procedure in Section 4.3.2 to organize construction into checkable intermediate goals. The figure groups the recorded checks into three display milestones and shows selected branches. At M1, the agent builds the platform, frame, and roof. The left branch fails because its upper ring misses the posts, whereas the other two displayed branches produce connected frames. Saving these passing scenes with their agent contexts allows exploration to continue from established structures.

At M2, the continuations add the interior and solar equipment. The right branch misplaces solar cells and fails the equipment check. The two continuations from the central M1 checkpoint pass, preserving the completed structure and equipment for finishing work.

At M3, the displayed continuations all start from the central equipped checkpoint. One leaves the glass opaque, obscuring the interior and failing the finishing requirements. The other two produce clear-glass renders and pass the full-task checks. Because the equipped checkpoint remains available, these finishing trials can address the remaining rendering requirements without rebuilding the frame or furnishing the cafe. The teal frames trace one retained path through all three milestones. Once its final result passes the original task verifier, the interaction prefix and successful continuations along that path form a complete demonstration. Failed siblings remain search records. This case shows how preserving checked intermediate work lets collection concentrate further trials on the unresolved part of a long task.

Together, the cases illustrate two ways to carry useful experience forward. TERRA reuses a procedure learned from earlier execution, while ORBIT BOTANICA reuses the work already completed in the software environment. Both routes direct subsequent attempts toward unresolved requirements and retain verified task trajectories for learning. Appendix C.2 details checkpoint contents, search budgets, skill records, and the treatment of complete paths and checkpoint continuations.

Summary.

The Experience Flywheel supplies the staged learner with both demonstrations and opportunities for fresh interaction. Curated grounding examples support control localization, while selected trajectories demonstrate complete workflows. RSI expands the candidate pool with attempts at difficult tasks. The same executable tasks can support new rollouts with task-specific outcome feedback as the policy develops. Section 5 explains how the learner uses these complementary resources. Appendix D describes data sources, scale, and source-grouped splits, with construction details in Appendix C.1.

5Staged Learning from Scalable GUI Experience

The Experience Library assembled by the Experience Flywheel provides quality-selected demonstrations of software work, alongside grounding examples and executable tasks for further collection (Section 4). The next step is to turn these resources into a policy that can reason about interfaces and carry out user goals across desktop and web applications. We design a three-stage learning pipeline that develops this capability progressively, as outlined in Figure 2.

  1. 1.

    Broad GUI mid-training first establishes familiarity with controls, application functions, and their effects through diverse software experience.

  2. 2.

    Verified long-horizon SFT builds on that foundation and concentrates learning on high-quality demonstrations that carry dependent work to completion.

  3. 3.

    Joint desktop–web agentic reinforcement learning then lets the policy learn from its own decisions and their outcomes in interactive environments.

Each stage uses the preceding policy as its starting point while changing the learning emphasis, from operational breadth to sustained completion and then outcome-driven improvement.

Table 3 summarizes the resources and priorities of the three stages. The shared interfaces of the NorthCUA Harness connect demonstration collection with online execution, so the policy can continue using the same observation and action conventions as training progresses. We describe each stage below. Appendix E defines the supervised prediction units and how recorded RL attempts become learning samples.

For model training, all spatial coordinates, including grounding targets and coordinate-based action arguments, use a shared [0,1000][0,1000] representation. For an image of width WW and height HH, a pixel location (x,y)(x,y) becomes (1000​x/W,1000​y/H)(1000x/W,1000y/H), giving the model a consistent coordinate convention across screen resolutions.

5.1  Broad GUI Mid-Training

Computer-use agents encounter many applications, interface layouts, and ways of performing similar operations. To work across these settings, a policy needs experience recognizing controls, interpreting their functions, and observing how actions change software state. We use broad GUI mid-training to build this foundation from diverse demonstrations (Wang et al., 2025c; Jung et al., 2026).

Through the collection routes in the Experience Flywheel, the reported broad task corpus contains over 100,000 trajectories and over 4 million GUI interaction steps, spanning dozens of applications and hundreds of operation families. This range exposes the policy to different tasks, materials, and interfaces within and across applications. We complement the trajectories with approximately 40,000 single-step grounding examples to train spatial recognition and control localization directly. The following collection and selection choices determine what experience enters this mixture.

Broad software coverage.

We select commonly used desktop applications and organize their functions into operation families. These profiles guide the task requests and CaseSpec environments used for experience collection, making it possible to vary the operations demonstrated within each application. Sampling across applications and operations, together with variation in source files and user goals, broadens this coverage. Representative coverage in the application profiles and workflow templates includes:

  • •

    Office work. Calc tasks cover formulas, auditing and reconciliation, filtering, pivot tables, and print layout. Writer adds document formatting and annotation, while Impress covers slide composition, content insertion, styling, and synthesis of source material into presentations.

  • •

    Visual and media work. GIMP tasks include cropping, resizing, annotation, and export. Inkscape adds vector text, color, alignment, and grouping operations. Image viewers, PDF viewers, and VLC provide content inspection and playback tasks.

  • •

    Workspace and information management. File-manager tasks cover organization and batch processing. Thunderbird, browsers, and VS Code add message handling, browser configuration, information lookup, and GUI-based file editing.

  • •

    CAD and 3D workflows. Expanded workflow templates define model review and part design in FreeCAD and SolveSpace, together with scene organization in Blender.

  • •

    Medical-image and anatomy visualization. 3D Slicer scenarios cover inspecting image volumes, checking orientation, annotating landmarks, and saving review scenes.

To extend this coverage beyond individual functions, we also use the long-workflow construction in Section 4.2.1. Its dependent tasks provide experience combining operations, carrying information between applications, and maintaining progress toward a shared deliverable. Mid-training therefore includes sustained workflows as part of its broad foundation, before the next stage concentrates on selected verified examples.

We further enrich web experience with (1) information retrieval, (2) form filling, (3) human-verification flows, and (4) frontend testing. Retrieval and form filling represent common everyday uses of websites. Human-verification flows add visually conditioned interactions encountered during web use, while frontend testing exercises the effects of controls and the persistence of state changes. Together, these settings diversify both what users ask and how an agent must interact, complementing desktop operation with web-specific workflows. The web scenario library also provides browser-game and sliding-puzzle tasks. Grounding examples add direct practice locating the requested control, including specialized controls handled by the documentation-guided route in Section 4.1. Table 4 summarizes the coverage of these sources, while Appendix D gives their rounded counts by domain.

Outcome-based trajectory curation.

Broad coverage is useful for learning only when the collected behavior provides a worthwhile demonstration. Large-scale attempts can also leave tasks incomplete or spend many actions without progress. We therefore use the agent-as-a-judge evaluator in Section 3.3 to inspect each candidate’s requested outcome, trajectory, and resulting artifacts or state (Zhuge et al., 2025). Its assessment selects completed work with useful execution behavior for the training corpus. This selection limits the inclusion of incomplete or low-quality traces while preserving examples of successful software use across the coverage pool.

Among the trajectories that pass review, selection preserves broad application and operation coverage. Meaningful exploration and recovery remain part of this experience when they lead to completed work, giving the model examples of how actions and subsequent observations inform the next decision. Outcome-based filtering thus makes quality control part of building a large and varied training corpus.

Learning localization, interaction, and assessment.

The selected mixture teaches both where to act and how to continue a task. For grounding examples, the model predicts the target control’s coordinates from the request and screenshot (Cheng et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). Trajectories train the model to predict each recorded assistant response from the task and the observations and history available at that decision. Targets include recorded reasoning, text responses, and action tool calls, while screenshots and tool results provide context. This response-level objective connects interpreting the interface, deciding what to do, and issuing the operation.

We also include evaluator trajectories as a separate judgment-task source. These examples condition the model on the evaluator’s inspection context and train its recorded assessment responses, providing demonstrations of how to check an outcome and support a judgment with evidence. Actor demonstrations retain their original decision-time context, separate from these evaluation inputs. The evaluator therefore serves two distinct purposes in mid-training: its reports select task demonstrations, and its own trajectories teach assessment. Appendix E.1 distinguishes the sample types and their response targets.

Through this broad mixture, mid-training develops familiarity with diverse GUI functions, action effects, and ways of interpreting results. This provides the operational foundation for learning more demanding workflows. The next stage sharpens that foundation using a concentrated set of high-quality, verified long-horizon demonstrations.

5.2  Verified Long-Horizon SFT

Mid-training gives the policy broad experience operating software, including extended workflows. Sustaining correct work over a long and difficult task requires a more concentrated learning signal: later decisions need to use earlier findings, preserve constraints, and complete the final deliverable. We therefore continue from the mid-trained checkpoint with supervised fine-tuning on selected long-horizon trajectories whose complete outcomes pass executable task verifiers (Yuan et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). The cohort contains approximately 3,000 trajectories and 310,000 GUI interaction steps.

Selecting verified demonstrations.

We start with tasks and executable checks supplied by Scaling Verifiers (Section 4.2.3) and collect successful completions. For difficult tasks that ordinary attempts do not solve, the skill-guided and milestone-guided RSI routes in Section 4.3 provide additional ways to obtain candidate demonstrations. Skills carry useful operating knowledge between attempts, while retained checkpoints let exploration build on completed intermediate work. In either route, a candidate enters this stage only after its final result passes the original task verifier. Appendix D lists the source contributions that remain to be reported separately from this aggregate cohort.

Within this accepted pool, we prioritize difficult workflows with long-range dependencies while maintaining application diversity. We use length to identify sustained work, then inspect how later actions use earlier results to assess its dependencies. We then check whether these demonstrations provide usable training sequences. Data cleaning rejects unusable records and traces with malformed or unmatched tool calls or unproductive loops. This screening retains coherent recovery when the trace shows an error, its correction, and verified completion. Each retained trace keeps its original action–observation sequence, preserving the context needed to learn that recovery. These checks combine programmatic outcome acceptance with demonstrations of purposeful work across stages.

Learning sustained completion.

With this selected corpus, we fine-tune the mid-trained policy to predict the recorded assistant responses from the request and decision-time context. The objective remains response prediction, but the data now emphasize maintaining task state, using intermediate results, coordinating work across applications, and recovering without losing the original goal. For assisted demonstrations, any supplied skill or milestone guidance remains in the context under which the recorded response was produced. Representation and sampling requirements are described in Appendix E.1.

This stage strengthens sustained task execution on top of the broad operational foundation. The resulting policy is the starting point for autonomous rollouts, where its own choices can create states absent from the demonstrations. Reinforcement learning provides the next learning signal by connecting those choices to their task outcomes.

5.3  Joint Desktop–Web Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Mid-training and long-horizon SFT provide a policy that can recognize interfaces and follow demonstrated workflows. To develop its ability further, we let it learn from autonomous interaction. Its own choices determine which states it encounters, and task outcomes provide feedback on whether those choices accomplish the user’s goal. We use agentic reinforcement learning to connect this fresh experience to policy improvement (Qi et al., 2025; Lai et al., 2026).

We train a single policy jointly on desktop and web tasks. The shared runtime in the NorthCUA Harness already expresses both as repeated observation, reasoning, and tool-based action, making it natural to learn from them through one training loop. Platform-specific observations and tools retain the differences needed to operate each interface. Task-specific verifiers then provide outcome feedback for the work performed in either domain.

Figure 24 follows an attempt from task preparation to a policy update. The Task and Environment Manager selects executable cases and prepares their isolated workspaces and verifiers, giving NorthCUA Rollout Workers the conditions needed to act with the current policy. Once those attempts have been recorded and scored, the Experience Adapter pairs the model calls with their task outcomes to construct training samples. These task-grouped samples let the Policy Learner compare alternative attempts with GRPO and update the shared policy (Shao et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025). Returning the new weights to the workers closes the loop, so subsequent interaction uses the updated model. The following subsections explain how we select useful tasks, obtain comparable feedback, and preserve executed decisions as that feedback enters learning.

5.3.1  Selecting Tasks with Outcome Variation

GRPO obtains its task-level learning signal by comparing the rewards of multiple attempts at the same task. An attempt’s relative outcome determines its advantage within that group. If all valid attempts receive the same terminal reward, their terminal group-relative advantages are zero. Since GUI rollouts are costly, we first identify tasks on which the SFT policy produces different outcomes, so initial collection can provide informative comparisons.

For each model, the Task and Environment Manager starts from human-reviewed desktop and web tasks associated with its SFT data. For each candidate case, we collect at least five rollouts under the SFT checkpoint with fixed task and execution settings. The task verifier scores each attempt’s outcome, and we select cases with variation among these valid verifier scores. Valid task outcomes determine this selection, while environment and verifier errors are recorded separately. This focuses RL collection on tasks where outcome feedback distinguishes alternative executions.

The selected cases form the initial RL task pool. Fresh grouped attempts supply the subsequent learning data. Appendix E.2 describes the screening protocol and the fields needed to record valid repeats and the selection rule for each run.

5.3.2  Joint Rollout and Task-Relative Feedback

With the task pool selected, we generate fresh attempts and turn their outcomes into the comparisons used by GRPO. For each case, the manager first establishes equivalent starting conditions. Workers then act in those environments, and the task verifier assesses each completed attempt. The recorded decisions and outcome are converted into samples for policy learning.

The Task and Environment Manager prepares a separate E2B sandbox for each attempt in a task group. All members receive the same request, initial files and application state, verifier, and execution budget. Their sandboxes are isolated, so one attempt’s edits do not change another’s starting conditions. This makes differences in outcomes interpretable as alternative executions of the same task.

NorthCUA Rollout Workers use the policy to carry out each multi-turn attempt. Desktop and web execution follow the same runtime loop, using their respective screen or browser observations and allowed tools. After execution, the manager runs the task verifier on the resulting workspace. Its valid verdict supplies the complete attempt’s terminal reward. Both successful and unsuccessful attempts contribute to the comparison, while setup or evaluation errors follow the separate invalid-attempt path.

The Experience Adapter binds each outcome to the model calls from that attempt. It reconstructs training samples from the recorded multimodal inputs and responses, retains behavior-policy likelihoods and versions, and marks which response tokens are learning targets. Each sample keeps its task and attempt identity so that the Policy Learner can compute relative advantages within the correct task group and apply the GRPO update. Desktop and web groups contribute to the same shared policy through this procedure.

This completes the path from an executable case to outcome-driven learning. For long GUI attempts, however, converting the record into training samples requires additional care. The next subsection explains the two rules we use to preserve both the original decision conditions and the attempt’s learning contribution during that conversion.

5.3.3  Preserving Executed Decisions for Learning

The rollout procedure provides complete attempts and their outcomes, but the learner must also preserve the conditions under which each decision was made. Our harness maintains a sliding window of recent screenshots and can compact earlier history. As a task proceeds, an image may leave the window or a summary may replace earlier messages. Using only the final history to train every response would therefore change the evidence available to some decisions. Preserving the sampled input is also a central concern in harnessed agentic RL (He et al., 2026).

To accommodate this context management, we design the Experience Adapter around two preservation rules. First, each response is learned with its recorded decision-time input, starting a new training segment when the history no longer extends consistently. Second, those segments retain the reward attribution and learning weight of their original complete attempt. This matters because frequent context changes can split one attempt into more segments than another. Figure 25 illustrates input preservation in panel (a) and attempt-level comparison and aggregation in panel (b). Together, the two rules let the harness manage long histories without turning a representation change into a different learning problem.

Preserve decision-time inputs.

Training associates each response with the context that produced it. To preserve this association through context changes, we capture each model call’s input, delivered response, generation log-probabilities, and behavior-policy version. The adapter joins consecutive calls only when their text and ordered image histories form a confirmed prefix extension under the same version. Image identity includes its content digest, so replacing a clean frame with the historical action overlay from Section 3.2.1 also breaks this prefix. The adapter starts a new segment from the captured input whenever images are replaced or evicted, a summary rewrites history, or the behavior version changes.

Earlier responses can still appear as history in a later segment, but they serve only as context there, following the history-masking principle used in ScaleCUA (Lv et al., 2026). Response masks assign each learning target to its original occurrence. Save is supervised when first generated and serves as context for Finish. This construction lets the learner use the harness’s actual decision conditions while keeping only new responses as targets. Appendix E specifies processor alignment and masks.

Preserve the complete attempt’s learning weight.

Preserving inputs can produce different numbers and lengths of segments across attempts. If these segments were treated as separate reward-bearing attempts, more frequent context changes would alter the group comparison. Averaging segment losses independently would also give an attempt more weight simply because it was split more often. Neither change reflects additional task experience.

We therefore retain the complete attempt as the comparison unit. GRPO computes its relative advantage once, and all of its segments receive that same value. In Figure 25b, the two segments of attempt 1 share A1A_{1}, while attempt 2 receives A2A_{2}. Loss aggregation then preserves the same unit. In the supported trajectory-mean configuration, we use the trajectory-level normalization also adopted in Qwen-CUA (Lu et al., 2026). We sum the masked policy losses over all target tokens of an attempt, divide by its total target-token count, and average these per-attempt means:

ℒpolicy=1N​∑i=1N∑s∈Si∑tmi​s​t​ℓi​s​tmax⁡(1,∑s∈Si∑tmi​s​t),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{policy}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{s\in S_{i}}\sum_{t}m_{ist}\ell_{ist}}{\displaystyle\max\!\left(1,\sum_{s\in S_{i}}\sum_{t}m_{ist}\right)}, (1)

where NN is the number of complete attempts, SiS_{i} contains the segments of attempt ii, mi​s​tm_{ist} selects target tokens, and ℓi​s​t\ell_{ist} is the token-level policy loss. All segments of an attempt enter the same optimizer step, so the denominator covers the complete attempt across microbatches. Appendix E defines the reduction and the run-specific optimization fields. This normalization prevents segmentation alone from increasing an attempt’s contribution when its target tokens and losses are unchanged. Combined with decision-time input preservation, it allows one continuous execution to yield several training segments without creating extra reward comparisons or increasing the attempt’s weight in the policy loss.

5.3.4  Continuous Rollout and Policy Updates

Training from long GUI rollouts is costly even after the samples are correctly constructed. Overlapping screenshot windows repeat visual preprocessing and carry large tensors to the learner. Meanwhile, task durations vary, so waiting for every active task before updating the policy can delay the next learning cycle. We address these two costs separately: visual-delivery mechanisms reduce redundant input preparation and transfer, while asynchronous coordination lets policy updates proceed without restarting ongoing tasks.

Deliver visual experience efficiently.

Adjacent decision windows often contain unchanged screenshots. Processing every window from scratch repeats work on those images. For a supported per-image processor, the Experience Adapter therefore reuses the preprocessing tensors of unchanged images within an attempt and processes only new images. It reconstructs the requested image order under the same processor settings. Changed images or settings require fresh processing. The reuse saves CPU preprocessing while retaining every image in the model input. The neural visual encoder still processes the complete visual input.

Large image tensors also add delivery cost after preprocessing. The object-store path supports lossless tensor compression, retaining a compressed payload only when it is smaller. The learner decodes the microbatch it is about to consume, recovering the same values, shape, and type. Bounded CPU workers prepare samples, and group admission counts completed work awaiting delivery so that preparation does not create an unaccounted queue. These mechanisms target redundant processing and payload transfer while preserving the sample’s contents. Appendix E.4 describes the implemented reuse and transport paths, their configuration, and the checks used to assess sample equivalence and delivery cost.

Coordinate policy updates asynchronously.

In asynchronous mode, completed groups can supply the learner while other workspaces remain active. To publish an update, the system pauses new model calls, waits for calls already in progress, commits the new weights, and resumes calls. Ongoing tasks keep their workspace and completed work, so later decisions can use the updated policy.

The captured behavior version and generation probabilities identify the policy that produced each response. A version change starts a new segment, so each policy ratio uses the corresponding behavior probabilities. For attempts spanning several versions, the clipped objective is an off-policy approximation. Preserving the recorded inputs keeps the sampled decisions identifiable, while policy lag affects the resulting update. Appendix E.2 defines policy lag and mixed-version attempts and distinguishes asynchronous coordination from synchronous collection. This coordination lets learning continue while ongoing tasks retain their environments and completed work.

Together, these mechanisms address the cost of supplying visual experience and coordinating updates, while the preceding preservation rules keep learning tied to the executed decisions and complete task outcomes. Section 6.5 reports the Mid-to-SFT checkpoint changes. Section 6.6 then examines joint RL through reported checkpoint comparisons, experience-delivery measurements, and a concrete example of task-relative feedback.

6Experiments and Analysis

Our evaluation follows the progression from identifying a control to completing a software task. We first compare grounding, desktop, and Web performance, then examine how results change through long-horizon SFT and joint desktop–Web RL. Trace analyses and selected cases connect these scores to concrete decisions, while an engineering profile measures the cost of delivering visual experience to the learner. Finally, we study NorthCUA-Ultrafast to assess how direct action selection changes the balance between task success and execution latency.

6.1  Evaluation Setup

Computer use requires both finding the right control and maintaining the user’s objective through successive state changes. We select the six benchmarks in Figure 1 to cover these complementary requirements. ScreenSpot-Pro tests dense professional interfaces, while OSWorld-G adds functional and spatial instructions. Desktop evaluation extends these decisions into application workflows, and Web evaluation covers both user tasks and defect detection. Table 5 summarizes what each benchmark measures.

Models and checkpoints.

We evaluate the NorthCUA family at three sizes, Nano (9B), Mini (35B), and Pro (397B), built on Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026a). We call the checkpoint after broad GUI mid-training Mid and the checkpoint after verified long-horizon supervision SFT. Thus, Mid already contains NorthCUA training. Mini and Pro use nominal 35B/3B and 397B/17B total/active language-model parameter counts, while Nano is dense. We keep the publicly released Qwen3.5 checkpoints separate as backbone-family references. The main grounding results use the long-horizon SFT checkpoints, while the main desktop, WebArena, and WebTestBench results use the final RL checkpoints. Ultrafast starts from the pre-RL Nano model. Dashes indicate unreported metrics. WebTestBench includes models with at least one measured metric. We report result metrics to one decimal, computing differences before rounding.

Grounding protocol.

We evaluate SSP by direct inference on the full screenshot, without iterative zoom or tool-assisted refinement, using all 1,581 examples. OSWorld-G uses 564 Refined instructions and normalized 0–1000 click coordinates. In addition to the main accuracy comparison, repeated predictions characterize consistency and target coverage. NorthCUA’s OSWorld-G entries use best-complete-run accuracy. Appendix I details the sampling settings and reports three-run means and standard deviations.

Interactive evaluation.

We use a maximum of 100 steps per task for OSWorld-Verified, WebArena-Verified, and WebTestBench, and 500 steps for OSWorld 2.0. OSWorld-Verified uses the officially supported 361-task setting, excluding eight Google Drive tasks that require separate account configuration.11 1 https://timothyxxx.github.io/OSWorld/user_guides/run_public_evaluation.html We evaluate OSWorld 2.0 on the full set of 108 tasks and retain binary completion, requiring a normalized score of 1, and mean partial score where available. We keep these measures separate because completing some requirements can still leave a dependent workflow unfinished. WebArena-Verified uses all 812 tasks and official outcome checks, with screenshots and structured page references as the agent’s observations. WebTestBench uses the golden-checklist setting, supplying the reference test items directly to the agent. This isolates interactive defect detection from checklist generation. We treat Fail as the positive class. Precision, recall, and F1 are computed within each task and then averaged separately across tasks, giving each task equal weight regardless of its checklist length.

Comparison models.

We select representative GUI specialists and general-purpose models from original papers and official model cards, including explicitly attributed evaluations of other providers’ models. Source markers distinguish our evaluations from published scores within each model group. Our OSWorld-G evaluation includes nine general-purpose baselines. Model-name citations identify original papers, reports, or official model pages, while Appendix I collects score sources and protocol details, including benchmark versions and action interfaces (Tong et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026a).

6.2  GUI Grounding Results

NorthCUA achieves state-of-the-art grounding results among the systems compared in Table 6, with Pro reaching 93.3% on SSP and 91.0% on OSWorld-G. The two benchmarks test complementary requirements, from locating small controls in dense professional interfaces to following functional and spatial instructions. We report the final long-horizon SFT checkpoints, using direct SSP inference and the Refined OSWorld-G instructions described in Section 6.1.

Claude Opus 5.5 is the strongest reference on both benchmarks in this comparison, scoring 88.1% on SSP and 89.9% on OSWorld-G in our evaluation. Pro exceeds these scores by 5.2 and 1.1 percentage points, respectively. On SSP, Pro also leads Qwen3.8-Max’s reported 84.5% by 8.8 points. On OSWorld-G, it exceeds Nex-N2.5-Pro’s reported 87.4% by 3.6 points.

The smaller tiers retain much of this capability. Mini reaches 92.4% on SSP and 87.9% on OSWorld-G with 35B total and 3B active language-model parameters. Its SSP score is within one percentage point of Pro. Nano reaches 72.9% and 83.0% with 9B parameters, with SSP accuracy close to GUI-Owl-1.5-32B-Instruct’s reported 72.9%. To understand what these aggregate scores capture, we next separate geometric precision, control semantics, and target availability.

Broad coverage and fine localization.

Mini and Pro both exceed 90% SSP accuracy in all six application groups. Pro reaches 95.0% in CAD and 94.5% in scientific software. This broad coverage also includes controls with little room for a coordinate error. To measure that difficulty directly, we pair the three models’ predictions on all 1,581 examples and group targets by size, measured as the smaller of the target box’s width and height in the original screenshot (Table 7). A target in the smallest group is less than 16 pixels wide or tall. On these narrow targets, accuracy rises from Nano’s 53.4% to Mini’s 85.2% and Pro’s 92.1%. Pro’s 6.8-point gain over Mini is larger than its 1.2-point gain on targets at least 32 pixels wide and tall. Its stronger aggregate result therefore also extends to the smallest target regions in this breakdown.

Interpreting specialized controls.

A small target must also be matched to the user’s intended function. Pro reaches 90.2% on SSP’s icon targets, followed by Mini at 88.6% and Nano at 55.0%. The difference persists within the most populous size band of 16–<32<32 pixels, where Pro and Mini both locate 89.0% of the 418 icon targets and Nano locates 53.1%. Their corresponding text-target scores are closer at 94.6%, 94.1%, and 84.6%, respectively. Even after this coarse size grouping, the gap between Nano and the larger models remains greater for icon targets than for text targets.

This distinction helps explain why our data construction addresses both target geometry and control meaning. The broad route retains the image coordinates, while documentation supplies functional descriptions for specialized controls.

Figure 26 illustrates this construction with the Legato Slide control in Ample Bass P, a virtual instrument hosted in FL Studio. Its articulation buttons encode different playing techniques through small symbols, so the icon alone gives little indication of the requested function.

The construction record links this control to the manual’s Legato Slide description (Ample Sound, n.d.) and generates the instruction Activate the Legato Slide articulation, retaining the original target location.

This documentation-grounded package was used in Nano and Mini training. In the SSP example, NorthCUA correctly locates the documented control from the full screenshot and query alone, without access to the manual during inference.

Target availability and repeated predictions.

Reliable grounding also requires recognizing when a requested target is absent. OSWorld-G tests this distinction alongside visible-target localization. Across three draws, Pro averages 91.7% on the 510 visible-target items, compared with Mini’s 88.6%. Its correct-refusal rate reaches 75.9% on the 54 absent-target items, compared with Mini’s 74.1% (Table 7). The larger gain is therefore in locating visible controls, while recognizing when to decline a location request remains harder across all three tiers. This distinction matters when a predicted coordinate becomes an agent’s next action.

Repeated sampling then reveals whether correct predictions persist across draws. Pro is correct in all three draws on 489 of 564 items, compared with 469 for Mini and 445 for Nano. Its pass@3 reaches 94.0%, covering 530 items, while its three complete runs range from 89.4% to 91.0%. Pro also succeeds at least once on 36 of Mini’s 53 persistently missed items, including 26 that Pro gets right in every draw. Thus, its stronger aggregate result accompanies both more stable successes and coverage of additional difficult items.

6.3  Desktop Agent Results

Grounding accuracy is useful only if the policy can sustain correct decisions until the requested software state is reached. Tables 8 and 9 therefore compare complete application workflows and longer dependent tasks. NorthCUA-Pro reaches 88.6% on OSWorld-Verified, the highest score among the compared systems. Mini reaches 85.3% with 35B total parameters, while the 9B Nano reaches 78.9%. These final RL results extend the grounding comparison from selecting individual controls to completing software tasks.

Pro exceeds Qwen-CUA-Max’s reported 87.6% by 1.0 percentage points and Qwen3.8-Max’s 86.1% by 2.5 points, using 397B total parameters against their reported trillion-scale sizes. At a smaller scale, Mini exceeds Nex-N2.5-Pro’s 82.2% by 3.1 points, while Nano exceeds MAI-Gym-9B’s 76.2% by 2.7 points. The comparison covers both general-purpose and GUI-specialized systems under the source-specific protocols in Appendix I. Section 6.5 examines how performance changes within the NorthCUA training pipeline.

OSWorld 2.0 extends the comparison to longer workflows with dependent requirements (Table 9). Binary completion tests whether all requirements are met, while partial credit records intermediate progress. Both measures increase from Nano through Mini to Pro in the final RL checkpoints. Pro reaches 30.6% binary completion and 66.8% partial credit on the full 108-task set. Within the 108-task reference block, these scores exceed GPT-5.6 Sol by 3.2 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively, under the listed evaluation protocols. The result combines higher earned credit with a higher rate of fully completed workflows. Section 6.5 examines how both measures develop through the NorthCUA training pipeline.

6.4  Web Agent Results

We next test whether accurate interaction supports complete requests on stateful websites. NorthCUA-Pro’s RL checkpoint reaches 73.9% on WebArena-Verified, the highest score in Table 10. Mini reaches 70.4%, while Nano reaches 67.2%, also after RL. We compare these results with published references and six additional general-purpose models evaluated by us. We then use the available trajectory exports to examine which website workflows are completed and where difficulties remain.

Pro’s score is 2.3 points above the joint-highest reference score of 71.6%, reported for Kimi-K3 and obtained by GPT-6 Astra in our evaluation. Mini reaches 70.4% with 35B parameters, exceeding Qwen3.8-Max’s reported 66.8% and Nex-N2.5-Pro’s 67.6%. Nano’s 67.2% provides a 9B alternative.

Coverage across websites.

Figure 27 examines trajectories across six website groups, using Nano and Mini after SFT and Pro after RL. Pro exceeds 70% success in each of the five single-site groups, reaching 84.0% on forums and 83.0% in store administration. This coverage spans consumer-facing websites and operational interfaces with editable records.

Cross-site tasks remain more demanding. Pro completes 17 of 48 tasks (35.4%), compared with 583 of 764 single-site tasks (76.3%). These workflows require carrying information or requirements between websites, making them a useful test of the sustained execution targeted by our long-horizon experience pipeline. The gap identifies cross-site coordination as a continuing challenge despite broad single-site coverage.

A complementary breakdown by requested outcome shows that Pro completes 274 of 374 state-changing tasks (73.3%), alongside 245 retrieval tasks and 81 navigation tasks. Thus, the result includes workflows that must leave a correct persistent site state, beyond locating or reading a page. Mini completes 253 state-changing and 223 retrieval tasks, compared with Nano’s 240 and 204. Its additional completions are concentrated in these two categories, while navigation counts are similar across the two models. Appendix I gives the group counts and the decision-length distributions for all three checkpoints.

Execution length and local setbacks.

The Pro export contains 14,604 model decisions across its 812 retained attempts. Successful attempts have a median of ten decisions. Of these, 24 contain at least 50 decisions, and the longest reaches 93. This range shows completion across both short interactions and extended workflows within the same benchmark.

For Pro, unsuccessful attempts have a median of 15.5 decisions and contribute 38.4% of the exported decisions despite accounting for 26.1% of tasks. Mini shows a similar concentration of work in failed tasks, whose median is 18 decisions compared with 10 for successes. Its 260 failures account for 50.6% of the 15,224 recorded decisions. This difference between successful and unsuccessful execution motivates our emphasis on feedback-guided correction during long workflows. Counts include terminal responses, with the record boundaries defined in Appendix I.

Section 6.7 illustrates such a correction in a Pro trajectory. The agent uses interface feedback to recover from an unavailable option while preserving the user’s date constraint.

Web testing.

Completing a user request and detecting defects require different judgments. We therefore evaluate defect detection on WebTestBench with the gold checklist supplied to each agent (Kong et al., 2026). Given these test items, the agent must exercise the application and distinguish genuine defects from correctly implemented behavior. Table 11 reports task-averaged precision, recall, and F1. NorthCUA-Pro achieves the highest F1 at 60.3%, exceeding the strongest comparison model, GPT-6 Astra at 58.2%, by 2.1 percentage points. At 35B, NorthCUA-Mini reaches 54.4% F1, improving on the same-size Nex-N2.5-mini by 5.8 points. Its precision and recall both increase by 6.3 points in this comparison, indicating gains in both the correctness of reported defects and the fraction of defects found.

The separate metrics clarify these detection profiles. NorthCUA-Pro also achieves the highest precision at 67.8%, alongside 63.7% recall. GPT-6 Astra combines the highest recall of 74.6% with 55.1% precision. GPT-5.6 Sol shows a similar emphasis on recall, at 70.3% against 54.8% precision, with an F1 of 56.1%. These differences distinguish finding a larger fraction of defects from making more accurate defect reports. We compute F1 separately for each task and report the mean of those per-task scores. The development case in Figure 18, separate from the scored WebTestBench evaluation, illustrates how such findings can guide a test–repair–retest cycle. Appendix F describes the browser-evidence qualification protocol.

6.5  Progress Across Training Stages

The final-checkpoint comparisons summarize benchmark performance. We next examine how the reported scores develop through training, beginning with the transition from broad mid-training to verified long-horizon SFT (Table 12). Desktop success increases across all three tiers, by 7.4 points for Nano, 15.0 for Mini, and 10.0 for Pro. Pro reaches 85.9% after this transition, while Mini shows the largest absolute desktop gain.

The Web results show a different distribution of gains. Nano improves by 9.2 points and Mini by 2.6, narrowing their gap from 10.5 to 3.8 points. Pro improves from 69.1% to 69.6%, a smaller gain of 0.5 points. The largest gains therefore depend on both model size and task domain. Mini gains most on desktop tasks, while Nano gains most on Web tasks. These checkpoint comparisons measure the complete training transition, including data selection and additional optimization. Appendix I records the available evaluation settings and aggregation rules for the stage comparisons.

The longer OSWorld 2.0 tasks expose the gap between partial progress and complete workflows at the Mid stage. Across the three tiers, partial scores range from 24.2% to 30.6%, while binary completion ranges from 0.9% to 9.3% (Table 12). Long-horizon SFT increases partial scores by 16.7, 20.7, and 33.0 points for Nano, Mini, and Pro, respectively. Binary completion also increases in every tier, with Pro rising from 9.3% to 27.3%. The gains therefore include more fully completed tasks as well as higher earned credit. These SFT checkpoints provide the starting points for the joint-RL comparison in Table 13, allowing the two training transitions to be examined separately.

From similar questions to verified source papers.

Figure 28 compares the same OSWorld 2.0 request in two NorthCUA-Mini runs before and after long-horizon SFT, focusing on how the agent selects and verifies source documents. A student has collected five question images and asks the agent to find their source exam papers. Similar statistical topics recur across sessions, so recognizing the topic alone can lead to a convincing but incorrect match. The third question, shown at the top of the figure, asks for an exponential-model test with specific null and alternative parameters.

The earlier run reads the question images and searches the candidate papers. It treats related exponential-test wording as confirmation and assigns Q3 to May 2025. Its final folder contains all five named PDFs, but the complete attempt receives 10% partial credit. The later run matches Q3’s specific test to December 2020 and checks that the copied file agrees with its source. This more discriminating search also appears elsewhere in the task. For Q5, it rejects a 15-mark candidate that differs from the requested 22-mark question, continues into Trash, and recovers the matching original paper. The resulting attempt receives full credit after 124 decisions, compared with 243 in the earlier run.

The contrast concerns what counts as completion. The earlier run assembles all five named PDFs while accepting an incorrect source match. The later run carries the question-specific criteria through search, rejection and final file checking. These observed behaviors illustrate the sustained verification targeted by long-horizon training. Appendix J gives the execution settings.

6.6  Joint Desktop–Web Reinforcement Learning

Long-horizon SFT teaches the policy to follow verified demonstrations. RL adds feedback on the states reached by the policy’s own actions, allowing successful and unsuccessful attempts at the same task to inform the next update. We examine this transition across desktop and Web execution under the shared training interface in Section 5.3. The prepared RL task pool contains approximately 1,500 desktop tasks and 500 Web tasks. Each model starts from its long-horizon SFT checkpoint and learns from fresh attempts on these tasks.

Task completion across platforms.

Table 13 compares each long-horizon SFT checkpoint (Before RL) with its subsequent joint-training checkpoint (After RL). Within each tier, the task set, tools, observation settings, and execution budget stay fixed, allowing the comparison to track performance through the transition from supervised learning to joint RL. OSWorld 2.0 retains Binary and Partial separately to distinguish complete workflows from progress on individual requirements.

After joint RL, reported success increases on both platforms at all three model sizes. OSWorld-Verified success rises by 2.9 points for Nano, 2.0 for Mini, and 2.8 for Pro. The corresponding WebArena-Verified gains are 3.0, 2.5, and 4.3 points. Pro reaches 88.6% and 73.9% on the two benchmarks, respectively. The desktop gains are similar across tiers, whereas Pro has the largest reported Web increase.

OSWorld 2.0 distinguishes gains in earned credit from gains in full-task completion. Partial scores increase by 4.7, 3.8, and 3.2 points for Nano, Mini, and Pro, respectively. Nano and Pro also improve binary completion by 0.9 and 3.3 points, with Pro reaching 30.6% binary completion and 66.8% partial credit. Mini’s binary score stays at 18.5% as its partial score rises from 46.3% to 50.1%. Together, the two metrics show where the final checkpoints improve requirement satisfaction and where that improvement also appears in complete workflows.

The remaining analyses address two different parts of the learning process. We first measure how the runtime delivers long visual records without changing their contents, then examine how task rewards distinguish two superficially similar interaction paths.

Delivering long visual experience efficiently.

The learning interface preserves the screenshots seen at each decision. As a result, long attempts can contribute repeated image windows across training segments. We use a separate archived 9B desktop run for the engineering profile and trajectory example below. To evaluate the lossless delivery path in Section 5.3.4, we examine 28 batches. Pairing the raw and encoded counters for each batch holds the underlying image tensors fixed while measuring their representation size.

Across this workload, encoding reduces the summed image-tensor payload by 97.2%, leaving 2.8% of the original representation size. The median raw and encoded batch sizes are 110.9 and 2.7 GiB, respectively. Encoding preserves all screenshots and their values. The counters cover eligible image tensors, including repeated segment occurrences, and exclude non-image fields and transport overhead.

Figure 29(b) reports delivery and policy-synchronization timings. Image encoding takes a median of 21.0 seconds, while object-store put calls take 1.9 seconds. The recorded policy-sync lifecycle takes 87.7 seconds and includes the 5.0-second in-flight call wait, weight export, rollout-engine reload, and receipt work. The in-flight wait is nested within the synchronization lifecycle, so these component timings are non-additive. They characterize delivery and synchronization costs, while the payload comparison measures the reduction in representation size for the same visual experience.

From interface choices to learning feedback.

Figure 30 examines what the terminal reward distinguishes in an actual task. The user asks the agent to switch Thunderbird to Tags view, hide the Get Messages button, and close the application to save the settings. This requires selecting the intended control and preserving its configuration after the application exits.

The two attempts follow the same first five actions and reach Tags view. Their next choices differ in scope. Attempt A disables the entire Folder Pane Header, removing all its controls from view. Attempt B opens the header’s own menu and unchecks Show Get Messages, leaving the remaining header controls visible. Both then close Thunderbird and report completion. The task verifier checks the saved Tags mode and the specific button’s hidden setting, returning reward 0 for A and reward 1 for B. Thus, the reward distinguishes the saved button configuration from hiding its entire parent header.

The complete group contains five successful and three unsuccessful attempts. Under the group-relative rule in Eq. 3, the successful attempts receive positive advantages and the unsuccessful attempts receive negative advantages, although their task reward is zero. These advantages carry the verifier’s distinction between saved configurations into the policy update. The recorded attempts also cross a policy-publication boundary. The learning interface in Section 5.3.3 preserves each segment’s input and behavior version while keeping its attempt reward and group identity. Checkpoint-level improvement is evaluated separately in Table 13.

6.7  An Evaluated Browser Recovery Case

Aggregate scores summarize completion, but a recorded interaction can show how the policy handles a mismatch between its plan and the interface. In the Pro episode in Figure 31, NorthCUA is asked to identify the best-selling brand in the first quarter of 2022. Reaching the answer requires navigating to the appropriate report, applying the correct time interval, and reading the returned product rows.

The first attempted period selection requests an unavailable Quarter option and times out. To identify the mismatch, the agent opens the dropdown. At decision 6, it observes that only Day, Month, and Year are available. It then uses Month for aggregation and enters January 1 and March 31 as the date bounds, preserving the requested quarter through the two date fields. By decision 10, the visible form contains the intended interval and is ready to run.

After running the report, the agent scrolls through its rows. The state at decision 12 shows two Sprite products among the highest-quantity entries. The agent checks the remaining rows before returning Sprite, and the saved task evaluator records success. The episode contains 13 model decisions, including the terminal response. Using the date fields with the available Month aggregation mode lets the agent correct its execution plan while preserving the requested quarter.

6.8  NorthCUA-Ultrafast

Long computer-use tasks accumulate the latency of many successive model decisions. Some decisions require open-ended content, but others reduce to choosing an operation and a control already present on the page. Predicting these finite choices directly could remove the decoding cost of routine actions. Jev provides a relevant interface for this purpose by answering structured choice questions without generating their answers token by token (Almeida, 2026). We adapt this idea to NorthCUA-Nano through NorthCUA-Ultrafast, which combines a choice head for finite decisions with the original model’s generation path for open-ended outputs.

Figure 32 illustrates the resulting division of work. The classifier receives the task and recorded interaction history, including page observations, screenshots, and action overlays. Candidate controls are bound to the latest valid page observation for execution. One backbone forward pass supplies the features used to score the operation and its applicable targets. A selected click, hover, or checkbox change can then be converted directly into a tool call.

Filling a field additionally requires text, so it triggers a new call using the original model prompt and generation head. Other tool actions and final responses use the same generation path. The executor validates the returned tool and arguments, and uncertain finite choices can fall back to native generation. This preserves the original output interface while allowing routine finite actions to bypass decoding. Appendix E.7.4 specifies the routing and validation profiles.
