We study how much adaptation this choice interface requires, starting from the long-horizon-SFT NorthCUA-Nano checkpoint before joint RL. Following Valen’s head-training approach (Liuziyu77, 2026), Head-only freezes all original weights and trains a 4.21M-parameter choice head, about 0.045% of the complete multimodal checkpoint. Head + LoRA also trains low-rank updates in the language layers (Hu et al., 2022), bringing the trainable total to 47.49M parameters. These adapters are enabled for classification and disabled for native generation, which keeps the original generator common to both variants. Both use about 226,000 training decision states, with fixed validation and test sets of 5,203 and 6,087 states. Supervision covers the recorded operation and its required target. Appendix E.7 gives the readout, training objective, and recipe.

We first evaluate whether the choice interface retains the recorded decisions. Head-only and Head + LoRA reach validation route-and-target accuracies of 86.1% and 88.2%, respectively. On the held-out test set, Head-only reaches 85.4% route-and-target accuracy against Full generation’s 85.0%, while their full-action exact-match scores are 64.0% and 64.6%. Generated parameters account for much of the remaining full-action error. The LoRA result is a validation comparison. Appendix E.7 gives the separate metrics and checkpoint-selection details.

To assess complete task execution, we compare the three policies on all 812 WebArena-Verified tasks, deploying each inference replica on a single GPU. Table 14 reports success and measured execution cost under the definitions in Appendix E.7.4. Success uses the full benchmark, while timing and step counts use a fixed 320-task subset selected from tasks jointly successful in the timing snapshot. Decoding bypass measures the fraction of dispatched actions produced directly by the choice head.

Head-only completes 481 tasks using only the choice head for adaptation. Head + LoRA completes 492 (60.6%), gaining 11 tasks or 1.4 percentage points. With about 0.5% trainable parameters, LoRA retains 94.4% of Full generation’s 64.2% success rate, leaving a gap of 3.6 percentage points.

The direct-action path is used frequently during execution. Head-only and Head + LoRA bypass generation for 40.2% and 31.1% of recorded actions, respectively. We next examine the task-level cost of these execution policies on the fixed success-selected subset.

Mean task time falls from 616.8 s to 288.8 s for Head-only and 266.8 s for Head + LoRA, despite slightly longer trajectories of 10.2 and 10.6 steps versus 9.45. On the fixed timing subset, this is a factor-of-2.32.3 reduction in mean task time for Head + LoRA. Its shorter task time despite a lower bypass rate also shows why direct-action frequency alone is insufficient to characterize execution efficiency. Each replica uses one GPU. Appendix E.7.4 gives the decoding and serving settings for these measured execution costs. The following case illustrates how fast selection and flexible generation cooperate within one successful task.

From search recovery to a saved product update.

Figure 33 follows a Head + LoRA attempt at a WebArena-Verified task that asks the agent to disable Karmen yoga pants because of quality issues. The request requires finding the correct catalog entry and saving its disabled state. Searching for the full phrase returns no records. The native generator responds to this observation by shortening the query to Karmen, after which the search exposes the configurable Karmen Yoga Pant and its individual variants.

The choice path opens the configurable product, switches Enable Product off, and selects Save, all without decoding action text. The final page shows the saved disabled state. The independent evaluator verifies the corresponding product-1819 save request and awards full credit.

Across the complete attempt, six of twelve executed browser actions bypass generation. The other actions handle navigation, query text, and waiting, and a thirteenth decision generates the final response. This execution illustrates the intended division of work. Generation remains available when the search needs revision, while discrete selections carry the recovered task through to a verified update. The aggregate bypass rates in Table 14 measure how often this direct execution path is used across the benchmark.

7Related Work

NorthCUA connects computer-use learning with the tasks and execution systems that supply its experience. We review these foundations in three parts. We first discuss policies and learning methods, then the construction of tasks and experience, and finally the harnesses and infrastructure that support their collection and use in training.

Computer-use policies and learning.

Accurate GUI actions depend on linking instructions to screen elements. SeeClick studies grounding pre-training (Cheng et al., 2024). GUI-Actor develops attention-based pointing, while GUI-Cursor refines cursor movements through visual feedback (Wu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). End-to-end policies build on this capability to coordinate actions over time. UI-TARS integrates perception, reasoning, and action prediction, and OpenCUA develops reflective supervision from human demonstrations (Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c). Learning from outcomes offers a further source of improvement. ComputerRL scales live-desktop RL (Lai et al., 2026), while VEM learns offline value estimates to guide environment-free policy exploration (Chen et al., 2026b). UI-TARS-2 and Qwen-CUA connect staged training with interactive learning (Wang et al., 2025a; Lu et al., 2026). For long trajectories, learning methods also specify how history and outcome feedback are carried across training segments. ScaleCUA masks reused history and shares rollout rewards and advantages across segments (Lv et al., 2026). Qwen-CUA preserves episode credit across slices and normalizes each trajectory’s objective over active policy tokens (Lu et al., 2026). NorthCUA combines broad GUI mid-training, verified long-horizon SFT, and joint desktop–web RL. Our emphasis is on integrating decision-time input preservation and complete-attempt weighting with the Harness and experience-production pipeline.

Scalable tasks and experience.

Scaling workflow learning creates a corresponding demand for executable tasks and reliable outcomes. OS-Genesis derives tasks from exploratory interaction (Sun et al., 2025), while GUI-360 combines sourced requests, environment templates, execution, and filtering for Windows data collection (Mu et al., 2025). ProCUA-SFT grounds tasks in real materials and checks preconditions before rollout (Jung et al., 2026). For outcome-driven learning, CUA-Gym and Qwen-UI-Agent synthesize compatible tasks, initial states, and verifiers (Wang et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026b). WEFT extends this whole-system view to tool-use post-training, using execution feedback to revise interacting components and fresh rollouts to evaluate each revision (Mao et al., 2026). NorthCUA organizes construction around available software and content, sourced requests, or verified seed tasks. Each route produces an executable CaseSpec . A separate grounding route uses application documentation to identify control functions and construct screenshot–query–location supervision.

Hard tasks also motivate retaining procedural knowledge across executions. Work2Skill turns synchronized human GUI demonstrations into reusable skills through on-demand inspection of action, visual, and available accessibility evidence (Huang et al., 2026). WebXSkill extracts executable procedures with language guidance from trajectories (Wang et al., 2026c). Search complements procedural guidance by considering alternative decisions. Computer-Using World Model simulates UI transitions for action selection (Guan et al., 2026), and Everything of Thoughts combines learned guidance with tree search for reasoning (Ding et al., 2024). Our RSI collection retains validated textual skills and real workspace checkpoints, so later attempts can reuse procedures or resume partial progress before full-task verification.

Agent harnesses and learning infrastructure.

Such collection and learning require an execution layer that preserves both software state and training evidence. UFO introduces hierarchical Windows interaction (Zhang et al., 2025c). UFO2 adds application-specialized agents and GUI–API integration (Zhang et al., 2026), and UFO3 extends orchestration to heterogeneous devices through a task DAG (Zhang et al., 2025d). For reuse across training systems, Agent Lightning v1.0 separates harness execution from RL optimization (He et al., 2026). Orchard provides shared sandbox lifecycle services (Peng et al., 2026), while Polar reconstructs token-faithful training trajectories from recorded model calls (Xu et al., 2026a). NorthCUA focuses on integrating these system responsibilities for stateful visual interaction. Its shared desktop/web runtime, live outcome inspection, and parallel lifecycle service support experience collection. The Experience Adapter then preserves the recorded decisions when converting online attempts into learning samples, connecting execution and assessment to policy training through the same task and outcome interfaces.

8Limitations and Responsible Use

Generalization and coverage.

NorthCUA operates across diverse applications, while unfamiliar software and changing interface conventions remain challenging. Documentation-guided grounding expands the functional knowledge available during data construction, and skill- and milestone-guided collection revisit workflows that ordinary attempts leave unfinished. Extending this coverage to new software and maintaining reliable execution as applications evolve remain important directions for the experience pipeline.

Feedback and optimization.

Executable verifiers and live-workspace inspection tie learning feedback to the work actually produced. Feedback quality depends on predicate coverage and the calibration of model judgments for open-ended content (Zheng et al., 2023). Controlled verifier probes and evidence-linked judgments help check both. Long workflows also concentrate many decisions into a terminal outcome. More informative intermediate feedback could improve credit assignment and help agents reach correct results with fewer unnecessary actions.

Responsible deployment.

Isolated workspaces, explicit tool profiles, and retained execution records provide controls for deployment. Operating real software also requires authorized access, least-privilege credentials, and confirmation for consequential actions. External pages and documents can carry indirect prompt injections (Debenedetti et al., 2024), motivating adversarial testing appropriate to each application. Released materials should undergo licensing, privacy, and credential review alongside the operational checks.

9Conclusion

We presented NorthCUA, an integrated system for developing computer-use agents through experience at scale. By connecting the NorthCUA Harness, Experience Flywheel, and Staged Learning through shared tasks and outcome checks, the system supports learning from both verified demonstrations and fresh policy interaction. Improved policies can return to the same infrastructure to collect further experience. Recursive self-improvement extends collection to difficult workflows by preserving useful procedures and verified milestones, allowing later attempts to build on earlier progress.

Across six benchmarks, the Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models in GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction. At 397B parameters, Pro outperforms the trillion-parameter general-purpose baselines on both grounding benchmarks, OSWorld-Verified, and WebArena-Verified. Stage comparisons further show improvements in desktop and Web execution across all three model sizes following long-horizon SFT and joint RL. Alongside these gains in task completion, NorthCUA-Ultrafast explores a complementary route to faster decision-making.

We release the three models, the full Harness code, and this technical report so that the work can be extended at both the policy and system levels. Together, they provide an open foundation for adapting agents to new software and developing better ways to collect and learn from experience. The broader goal is to make reliable software execution a general AI capability, allowing users to delegate complete workflows from intent to verifiable outcome.

Appendix A Implementation and Reproducibility

The executable task, its workspace, and the resulting learning samples share an attempt identity. CaseSpec binds the request to its materials, initial state, and execution settings. The environment service manages the workspace, the NorthCUA Harness records interaction, and the configured verifier or evaluator establishes the outcome. The Experience Adapter retains the policy’s decision-time inputs when constructing samples, and the learner associates those samples with their attempt-level feedback.

A.1  Information and Permission Boundaries

Construction, execution, evaluation, and learning use different information. The generator can inspect construction metadata, while the acting policy receives the request and permitted task inputs. Host-only acceptance criteria remain with evaluation. Tool capability checks control permitted operations, while input construction and sample extraction separately control which information each role receives.

Actor and evaluator records remain separate, preserving the actor’s submitted result and decision-time inputs during inspection. Actor imitation excludes privileged evaluation calls. Evaluator demonstrations used in mid-training are separate judgment tasks with their own inspection context (Appendix E.1). During ordinary execution, the actor receives the task request and permitted inputs, while construction dependency graphs remain construction metadata. Runtime profiles, live-inspection rules, and resource ownership are detailed in Appendices H.1, H.1, and H.3.

Appendix B Grounding Data Details

Section 4.1 describes visual, structural, and documentation-grounded labeling. The common annotation unit links an unannotated screenshot, a visible control, its target geometry, and one or more queries. Documentation supplies functional evidence, while the GUI image supplies the target location.

Crop and resize transforms preserve correspondence with the original screen. A point target lies inside the actionable region, without an occluding foreground element. A menu-item target requires the item to be visible in the captured menu state. Queries requiring unprovided hidden state are excluded. Diagnostic boxes and action annotations are kept separate from the unannotated grounding input.

Documentation matching checks the control’s appearance, nearby controls, visible application state, and the manual’s applicability. Ambiguous or version-incompatible matches remain outside the accepted set. Label checks distinguish a wrong function from a spatial miss, even when both refer to similar-looking controls. We count source images, target controls, and query variants separately, grouping paraphrases with their original target. Source grouping and split rules are shared with Appendix D.

Appendix C Task Construction Details

The construction routes in Section 4 bind a request, usable materials, an initial workspace, and acceptance conditions into an executable task. A material record combines file format, bounded content summaries, and provenance. After selection, the workspace builder copies the inputs and records their content hashes and initialization procedure. The task distinguishes read-only inputs, distractors, mutable targets, and required outputs.

For dependent work, the plan connects producers to the artifacts or services consumed by later stages. Structural checks reject unknown predecessors, cycles, disconnected stages, incompatible references, and required outputs without production stages. Host-only evaluation artifacts remain with the evaluator. These constraints define valid dependencies while leaving the actor free to choose GUI actions within the task’s prerequisites. The following details cover environment preparation, assisted collection, and verifier test states.

C.1  Environment Construction and Binding

The request-conditioned desktop builder first filters candidate materials by format and application requirements, then ranks them by content. Request refinement uses the selected inputs to make references concrete while preserving the source goal and constraints. A mismatch between the request and available materials sends the task back to construction. Content summaries support selection without replacing inspection of the files being packaged.

EnvAgent finalizes the workspace against a current report of file evidence and query alignment. Material changes require renewed inspection before finalization. The compiler retains packaged paths, checksums, environment configuration, and startup actions, with ownership and permissions that make the initialized files accessible to the desktop user. The specified live-validation procedure additionally checks GUI opening and required operations in an isolated attempt. Collection begins from a fresh initialization, preserving the specified starting state for the actor.

Dependency checks distinguish data flow from required workflow order. For example, the office plan in Figure 14 uses content from A and B in its final PDF, while the record update in C has an independent acceptance condition. The C-to-D edge imposes order without making the record a source of PDF content. A designated terminal artifact therefore need not be the task’s only required result.

Reference-based web construction specifies both the visible interface and the state supporting its interactions. Its environment description records the reference source, supported pages and operations, observed versus generated content, backend schema and seed state, reset procedure, and external dependencies. Rendering, navigation, persistence, initialization, and task feasibility are checked separately against this description. It defines the reconstructed pages and behaviors used for task collection. Appendix D summarizes the resulting data sources and scale.

C.2  Hard-Task Collection Protocol

The two collection routes in Section 4.3 retain different products between attempts: validated operating guidance and recoverable execution progress. Selection starts in the training partition after ordinary attempts expose a useful obstacle. Invalid environments, ambiguous requirements, and unreliable verifiers are repaired or excluded before further exploration. The task’s final acceptance conditions remain fixed as candidate skills and intermediate milestones evolve.

A skill record identifies its task family, applicability, guidance, version, source attempts, validation cases, and known failures. Validation uses a frozen candidate, separate from the attempts that produced it. Task-specific assistance, reuse within a family, and transfer to a new application remain distinct uses of the record.

For milestone search, a planning agent may inspect the request and verifier to define dependent subtask–check pairs. Actor-visible guidance uses only permitted task information. Hidden predicate constants and expected answers stay in evaluation context. A checkpoint binds the environment snapshot to its parent attempt and action prefix, prompt-visible history, summary, notes, skill and milestone guidance, model/tool configuration, and remaining budget. Restoration re-establishes device bindings and obtains fresh observations. External service state needs its own isolation and restoration mechanism.

A candidate actor state is retained before state-changing inspection. Such inspection uses an evaluation copy or separate branch and receives its own action record. Actor continuations resume from the retained pre-inspection state. The checkpoint record retains enough ancestry to reconstruct the selected path and the information available at each decision.

Search configuration specifies candidate counts, state selection, diversity and retention limits, uncertainty handling, and stopping rules. Its budget includes failed attempts, skill validation, snapshot/branch operations, inspection, and live-resource costs. A selected recoverable failure retains its unresolved milestone label until its continuation repairs that requirement. Local checks guide expansion, while the original task verifier determines full-task acceptance.

Training extraction follows the selected actor path. Search-controller decisions, snapshot operations, and failed sibling branches are excluded from actor targets. Supplied skills and milestone guidance remain in the context that conditioned those targets. Cross-branch knowledge transfers are recorded at their point of use. Deleting this guidance would change the decision inputs, so an unguided demonstration requires recollection.

A complete assisted path, a checkpoint-conditioned continuation, and a verified subtask from an incomplete attempt are different sample types. Unassisted completion is evaluated in a fresh-start run using the original task inputs. Their counting units and source-family separation follow Appendix D.

C.3  Controlled Verifier States

Verifier tests hold the intended obligations fixed while varying the submitted state. An incomplete initial state is a negative control, a correct result is a positive control, a near miss isolates one violation, and a valid alternative tests sensitivity to presentation. Each test retains the initial and final state, protected inputs, acceptance conditions, and the expected verdict. Testing score composition with stipulated predicate values is separate from executing the predicates on actual artifacts.

Figure 34 gives a concrete regional-report example. Expected gross sales are North 420 and South 380, totaling 800. Acceptance also requires complete regional content, template compliance, and unchanged protected source files. The two accepted presentations satisfy all of those conditions, including the regional content and protected-file requirements.

Appendix D Training Data Sources and Scale

The dataset records distinguish source materials, constructed tasks, execution attempts, accepted trajectories, extracted samples, and training consumption. A task can produce several attempts, and a trajectory can produce several prediction units. Grounding images, target controls, and query variants use their own units. Table 16 summarizes the supervised data by stage and domain using rounded counts.

Together, the desktop and web sources provide over 100,000 trajectories and over 4 million GUI interactions for mid-training. The long-horizon SFT cohort contains approximately 3,000 queries and 310,000 interaction steps.

These rounded counts summarize source cohorts by stage and domain before model-specific sampling and repeated consumption. Auxiliary evaluator demonstrations are accounted for separately from task-execution trajectories.

A sample’s lineage connects source and task family, environment and fixture identity, collection policy, permitted tools, outcome check, and extraction version. A consumed training sample additionally identifies its training shard and stage. Actor episodes and evaluator judgment episodes retain separate roles and permissions. Complete assisted paths, checkpoint continuations, and verified subtask demonstrations also retain distinct sample types.

Related screenshots, documents, material sets, task seeds, source sites, repository/issue families, and derived skills are grouped before splitting. Source-policy disclosure, licensing, and access permissions apply to each supervised source.

Appendix E Model Identities and Learning Details

The Nano, Mini, and Pro tiers use the Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B backbone variants, respectively (Qwen Team, 2026a). Table 17 lists the backbone identities and their language-model parameter counts. The mixture-of-experts variants have distinct total and activated counts.

The results use Mid for broad GUI mid-training and SFT for verified long-horizon supervision. Mid is already a NorthCUA checkpoint, distinct from an upstream pre-trained release. The supervised stages differ in their source mixture and selection criteria. We first describe the supervised prediction units, then explain how task-group feedback and recorded RL attempts become learning samples.

E.1  Supervised Representation and Sampling

The supervised stages share response prediction but use different sources and selection rules. An extraction map Φ\Phi converts a grounding example, task trajectory, or evaluator episode into prediction units x∼𝒟x\sim\mathcal{D}. A unit can be a decision or a context-bounded slice. For a binary target mask mtm_{t} with ∑tmt>0\sum_{t}m_{t}>0, the conditional objective is

ℒsup=−𝔼x∼𝒟​[1∑tmt​∑tmt​log⁡pθ​(xt∣x<t)].\mathcal{L}_{\rm sup}=-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\frac{1}{\sum_{t}m_{t}}\sum_{t}m_{t}\log p_{\theta}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\right]. (2)

Here x<tx_{<t} includes the recorded multimodal input at that decision. The expectation is over extracted units after source sampling, so an episode’s weight depends jointly on extraction, sampling, and the within-unit mean.

Grounding examples target coordinates. Actor trajectories target recorded assistant responses, including reasoning, text, and tool calls according to the target mask. Evaluator episodes are separate judgment tasks targeting inspection and assessment responses from their own permitted context. Grounding, actor trajectories, and evaluator examples enter mid-training. Long-horizon SFT uses task trajectories. The three sources have separate counts and sampling weights.

An actor input contains the request and the observations, tool results, summaries, notes, and guidance available at that decision. Post-execution judgments and hidden acceptance values belong to the evaluation context. A post-action screenshot or action overlay is available only to later decisions. Actor-issued note calls remain in the response stream with the mask specified by the recipe. Construction-agent and privileged evaluator calls are outside actor targets.

Sampling determines how source and episode lengths influence learning. Uniform decision sampling, uniform trajectory sampling, and token-weighted sampling give different weights to long episodes. The recipe therefore distinguishes extraction, source/domain weighting, packing, target deduplication, and loss reduction. A response repeated as context has one target occurrence. Assisted traces retain the skill or milestone guidance that conditioned them. These supervised choices are specified separately from online RL assembly.

Selection precedes sampling. Broad trajectories come from judge-selected completed tasks. Long-horizon trajectories require original full-task script acceptance followed by execution-quality and dependency checks. Skill- and milestone-assisted trajectories undergo the same checks. Cleaning rejects unusable records. Retained episodes preserve action–observation alignment, including coherent recoveries. Source attribution and cohort overlap follow Appendix D.

E.2  Task Groups and Terminal Feedback

The initial RL pool follows Section 5.3.1: human-reviewed desktop and web tasks are screened with at least five attempts under each model’s SFT checkpoint and fixed execution settings. Selection uses variation among valid verifier scores, with environment and verifier errors recorded separately from task outcomes. Fresh grouped attempts on the selected pool provide the learning data.

Members of a group attempt the same case package from equivalent initial states under the same verifier and budget. A task-script result can be a finite numeric reward or an interpretable Boolean/status verdict, with Boolean fallback mapped to zero or one. Reward ranges and preprocessing remain task-specific. Script errors, timeouts, nonzero exits, and uninterpretable results follow the invalid-evaluation path. Valid negative verdicts remain learning outcomes.

Retries retain logical member identity under the configured retry policy. Complete-group checks prevent missing members from silently changing the comparison. Domain sampling weights specify scheduled work, while completed, admitted, and consumed members describe successive stages of actual use. The logical attempt remains the unit of group membership, independently of infrastructure retries or the number of extracted training segments.

For G>1G>1 valid members, terminal advantages are

Ai=Ri−R¯sR+ϵ,R¯=1G​∑i=1GRi,sR2=1G−1​∑i=1G(Ri−R¯)2,A_{i}=\frac{R_{i}-\bar{R}}{s_{R}+\epsilon},\qquad\bar{R}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}R_{i},\qquad s_{R}^{2}=\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{i=1}^{G}(R_{i}-\bar{R})^{2}, (3)

where RiR_{i} is the attempt’s terminal reward and ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}. The baseline is computed within the task group, independently of other tasks or domains. Identical rewards produce zero terminal advantages. Each attempt contributes one advantage shared by its segments. The trajectory-mean configuration uses the full attempt’s target-token denominator in Eq. 1.

Synchronous and asynchronous execution differ in when work can overlap policy updates. For asynchronous runs, policy lag is the learner version at consumption minus the behavior version of each call. Lag and the fraction of mixed-version attempts describe the executed configuration.

E.3  Clipped Policy Objective

Let b⁡(s)b(s) denote segment ss’s captured behavior version, and let hi​s​th_{ist} contain its multimodal context and generated prefix before token xi​s​tx_{ist}. The learner uses the PPO-style clipped surrogate (Schulman et al., 2017) with the member advantage from Eq. 3:

ρi​s​t\displaystyle\rho_{ist} =exp⁡(log⁡πθ​(xi​s​t∣hi​s​t)−log⁡πb⁡(s)​(xi​s​t∣hi​s​t)),\displaystyle=\exp\!\left(\log\pi_{\theta}(x_{ist}\mid h_{ist})-\log\pi_{b(s)}(x_{ist}\mid h_{ist})\right), (4)
ℓi​s​tclip\displaystyle\ell_{ist}^{\rm clip} =−min⁡{ρi​s​t​Ai,clip⁡(ρi​s​t,1−δ−,1+δ+)​Ai}.\displaystyle=-\min\{\rho_{ist}A_{i},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{ist},1-\delta_{-},1+\delta_{+})A_{i}\}.

The likelihoods use the temperature and recorded-support convention in Appendix E.6. The parameters δ−\delta_{-} and δ+\delta_{+} define the lower and upper clipping widths, respectively. In the trajectory-mean configuration, Eq. 1 aggregates token losses within each complete attempt before averaging attempts.

A behavior version is constant within a segment, but an asynchronous attempt can span several versions. Captured likelihoods identify the denominator for each response. For attempts spanning policy versions, the clipped update is an off-policy approximation under policy lag and changing state distributions. Terminal feedback assigns one attempt-level advantage across the episode. Local process rewards and distillation are separate extensions to this terminal-reward recipe.

E.4  Visual Experience Delivery

The delivery mechanisms in Section 5.3.4 address repeated CPU image preparation and visual-tensor transfer. They preserve the learner’s inputs, unlike semantic compaction, which changes those inputs. Lossless tensor encoding reduces transfer volume. CPU preprocessing reuse is a separate mechanism whose enablement depends on processor compatibility.

The preprocessing-reuse path supports the Hugging Face Qwen2-VL processor’s independent per-image outputs. Within a member, it retains pixel_values and image_grid_thw under fixed processor settings, reconstructs the requested image order, and processes new content. A clean-to-overlay replacement or a configuration change requires fresh processing. Unsupported processors or incompatible output structures use ordinary processing. The cache stores CPU tensors, while neural visual encoding remains part of the model forward pass.

Owned per-image storage avoids retaining an obsolete batch through a view. The member’s window is cleared on exit, and state publication remains scoped to that member during cancellation. Tensors already staged for prompt projection can be reused during training materialization under the same content and processor identity.

The selected transport path uses Zstandard level 1 on contiguous CPU image tensor bytes after data-parallel partitioning. An encoding replaces the original only when smaller. A failed encoding leaves the original available. The consumer checks the expected byte count, decodes its selected microbatch, and transfers tensors to the accelerator without retaining a decoded full-batch cache. Dtype, shape, resolution, and floating-point values remain unchanged.

Payload accounting includes delivery-pending groups as well as reserved, active, and ready work. Admission limits are expressed as numbers of groups. Successful compact object-store transfer allows the producer to release visual references, while consumption records keep sample identities without those payloads. The data-parallel delivery barrier remains in place.

Equivalence checks compare prompt tokens, image order, preprocessing tensors, dtype, shape, masks, rewards, and behavior likelihoods on the same captured calls. Full-update comparison additionally fixes model, optimizer, random state, and partition schedule. Component measurements cover preprocessing, codec, transfer, and memory costs. The complete optimizer interval is a separate measurement boundary.

E.5  Sequence Integrity and Update Boundaries

Before assembling an actor RL segment, the adapter checks the delivered-response receipt, policy/tokenizer/template/processor identities, call order, and response digests. It admits main-agent calls only. Terminal Controller evidence confirms delivery by linking ordered execution steps and their artifact digests to the captured responses. Task success is established separately by the outcome check.

Calls can be appended when prompt tokens and ordered media bindings confirm a prefix extension under the same behavior version. Media identity includes a content digest. Replacing a clean frame with an action overlay, evicting an image, rewriting history, or changing behavior version therefore starts a new segment from the newly captured input. Responses repeated as history provide context and are masked out of the new segment’s targets. Their original target occurrences remain available for learning. Processor-specific visual-position projection preserves captured image content and order.

Segments from the same logical attempt share its identity and reward provenance. The adapter checks group completeness before computing advantages. In the trajectory-mean configuration, the learner sums target token counts over the full attempt before partitioning. Every segment uses this denominator within the same optimizer step. Partition invariance holds when conditioning, masks, and token losses stay fixed.

Weight publication pauses new model calls, drains calls already in progress, commits the new weights, and resumes calls with the new behavior version. The tasks themselves can remain active in their workspaces. After abnormal recovery, execution restarts from committed checkpoint and cursor state, rebuilding warm queues and unfinished rollouts from that committed state.

E.6  Sampling Likelihood Convention

The policy ratio requires compatible learner and behavior likelihoods. For temperature T>0T>0 and the recorded behavior support Sb​(h)S_{b}(h), the likelihood convention is

pθ(T,Sb)​(x∣h)=𝟏{x∈Sb(h)}exp(zθ(x∣h)/T)∑u∈Sb​(h)exp⁡(zθ​(u∣h)/T).p_{\theta}^{(T,S_{b})}(x\mid h)=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{x\in S_{b}(h)\}\exp(z_{\theta}(x\mid h)/T)}{\sum_{u\in S_{b}(h)}\exp(z_{\theta}(u\mid h)/T)}.

Here hh contains the captured context and generated prefix, and zθz_{\theta} denotes the learner’s logits. With top-p equal to one and no other vocabulary restriction, Sb​(h)S_{b}(h) is the full vocabulary. For nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2020), replay uses the recorded token identities and offsets at each target position rather than constructing a new nucleus from current learner logits. Temperature, support capture, and replay settings belong to the run configuration. Entropy regularization has a separately configured support mask.

E.7  NorthCUA-Ultrafast Adaptation and Evaluation

This section details the choice-based execution mode introduced in Section 6.8. Its training unit is a decision state extracted from a WebAgent trajectory. The original causal prefix supplies the input, and the following recorded action supplies the label. The classifier and native generator use this same underlying evidence through different prompts.

E.7.1  Multimodal Inputs and Action Routing

The classification prompt retains the task, preceding actions, tool results, screenshots, and action overlays. It replaces the original system instruction with a finite-choice instruction and appends the current operation and target candidates. Native generation instead uses the original messages, tool schemas, and chat template, keeping the original action prompt separate from classification-specific instructions and selections.

Targets come from the latest valid set-of-mark observation. We exclude explicitly disabled elements and restrict filling to input-like roles and checkbox changes to checkbox roles. At most 150 elements are retained per observation, with the number omitted recorded. A finite operation is offered when its tool and eligible targets are available. Selection operates over this retained candidate set. Table 18 gives the seven routes. The operation and each available target type form separate variable-size choice questions. Only the chosen operation’s target is used for execution.

In the offline full-action evaluation below, generation starts with a fresh input encoding and cache, with any LoRA adapters disabled. Decoding is greedy with thinking disabled and at most 4,096 new tokens. A valid result requires model termination and the relevant tool schema or response structure. Strict routing rejects FILL target disagreements. NATIVE accepts a valid offered tool, including a finite-action tool if the original generator selects one. This matters when comparing route labels with complete actions below.

E.7.2  Readout and Training

The last hidden layer supplies four vectors for each candidate. These are the mean context representation before the appended choice block, the mean question-instruction representation, the mean candidate representation, and the final decision-marker representation. Each vector has dimension 4,096. A shared head normalizes and projects these roles to width 512, adds learned role embeddings, and applies two Mixer blocks. Each block mixes the four roles through a →→44\!\rightarrow\!16\!\rightarrow\!4 MLP and the channels through a →→512512\!\rightarrow\!1024\!\rightarrow\!512 MLP. A scalar readout from the updated candidate role supplies its score. Softmax is applied within each question, and argmax selects its answer. The Mixer operates within each candidate’s four roles, while the backbone has already encoded the full candidate list.

For state ii, let QiQ_{i} contain the supervised operation question and, when required, the corresponding target question. With correct candidate yi​qy_{iq}, score zi​q​kz_{iqk}, and candidate set Ci​qC_{iq}, the objective for a minibatch of decision states ℬ\mathcal{B} is

ℒchoice=1|ℬ|∑i∈ℬ1|Qi|∑q∈Qi−logexp⁡zi​q​yi​q∑k∈Ci​qexp⁡zi​q​k.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{choice}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{1}{|Q_{i}|}\sum_{q\in Q_{i}}-\log\frac{\exp z_{iqy_{iq}}}{\sum_{k\in C_{iq}}\exp z_{iqk}}. (5)

Averaging within each state keeps states with an operation and target equally weighted with operation-only states. Other target questions receive no label, and the original output tokens receive no generation loss.

The dataset contains 225,710 training, 5,203 validation, and 6,087 test states from 25 trajectory collections. Normalized task goals define groups, and the fixed holdouts remain unchanged when training sources are expanded. Filtering removes stale or missing targets, conflicting labels, invalid actions, and known target-tool errors. The native multimodal prefixes are rejoined to their source records before training. Both input paths are checked against a 73,728-token budget after image-token expansion, without truncation. Grouping removes identified request duplicates. Semantically related paraphrases and task templates may still occur across groups.

AdamW uses β=(0.9,0.999)\beta=(0.9,0.999), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, and weight decay 0.01, with no learning-rate warmup or schedule. Candidates retain deterministic ID order, without shuffling or class reweighting. Head + LoRA adds 43.278M adapter parameters to the same 4.214M head. The adapters remain unmerged so that generation can disable them. The two variants share data, logical batch size, and seed, but use different completed budgets. Checkpoints are selected by full-validation joint accuracy, then loss and earlier epoch.

E.7.3  Offline Decision and Action Results

Route-and-target joint accuracy requires all labeled questions for a state to be correct. It excludes generated text and other open-ended parameters. Full-action exact matching instead compares the tool name and complete arguments, or the final response object, with the reference action. It normalizes reference IDs to strings, then compares tool names, parameter values, and response text exactly. A NATIVE route can still generate the correct finite-action tool call, so full-action matching can credit a decision whose route label differs from the reference.

Head-only correctly selects the route and target in 5,196 test states, compared with 5,172 for projected full generation. Complete-action matching is lower for the hybrid policy, at 3,897 versus 3,933 states. In the paired comparison, 3,757 states match under both policies, 140 only under Head-only, and 176 only under full generation.

The hybrid gains 46 exact matches among 2,576 CLICK states, while losing 25 among 906 FILL states and 30 among 2,087 NATIVE states. Losses on generation-dependent FILL and NATIVE actions exceed the gains on CLICK.

The diagnosis is clearest among the 1,403 states with a correct Head-only route but an incorrect hybrid action. Of these, 935 have mismatched parameters for the same tool, 359 have a tool/final-output kind mismatch, 18 differ in final JSON fields, and 91 are rejected by route or target consistency checks. These are reference-matching outcomes, distinct from environment success. The paired test reuses one saved native generation per state for both policies, including states whose hybrid action bypasses generation. Its execution time covers this shared-generation offline procedure.

Validation selects epoch 1 for Head + LoRA and epoch 22 for Head-only. At the same completed epoch 13, their joint accuracies are 86.9% and 85.5%, respectively. This provides an equal-epoch comparison, alongside the selected checkpoints in Table 20. All results come from one training seed, and states can share a task. Earlier text-only experiments use a different input protocol and are excluded from this multimodal comparison.

E.7.4  Online Task Completion and Timing

The online comparison adapts the long-horizon-SFT NorthCUA-Nano checkpoint before joint RL and retains the original WebAgent runner. Each inference replica occupies one GPU. Full generation sends every decision through the native generation path. Both Ultrafast variants and the case in Figure 33 use the generation-preferred profile with a finite-choice confidence threshold of 0.8. A direct action requires both its operation and target probabilities to meet this threshold. Lower-confidence selections, missing or stale current references, and unsupported observation surfaces defer to native generation. When generation is used, its complete valid action is accepted without replacing its arguments with the classifier’s selection. The gateway records any disagreement. This differs from the strict agreement checks used in the offline comparison above.

Task outcomes and matched execution records.

The evaluator assigns success to 521, 481, and 492 of the 812 tasks for Full generation, Head-only, and Head + LoRA, respectively. Failures, timeouts, and evaluation errors remain in the denominator. The latest Head-only and LoRA scores come from rescoring existing trajectories. Their efficiency statistics retain the same execution records.

Task time and trajectory length use a fixed matched subset of 320 tasks, selected from 343 tasks jointly successful in the timing snapshot. The remaining 23 lack complete timing or action-dispatch evidence for at least one policy. This fixed set supports comparisons on the same tasks and defines the population for the conditional means. Rescoring updates the success totals while leaving this timing population unchanged.

Step and action boundaries.

A step is one decision round, including a final response. Classification followed by generation or a length retry remains one step. An action counts a tool call dispatched to its handler, including calls that subsequently fail during execution. A step may issue multiple actions or none, and a final response is not a tool action. Only the final selected attempt is counted. The 320-task set contains 3,025, 3,260, and 3,386 steps, respectively, yielding the means in Table 14. Its dispatched-action totals are 2,683, 2,940, and 3,066, with means of 8.4, 9.2, and 9.6 actions.

Decoding bypass counts recorded dispatched actions produced directly by the choice head without invoking native generation. The fractions are 6,182/15,385 for Head-only and 4,248/13,652 for Head + LoRA, or 40.2% and 31.1%. These denominators cover available actions from successful and failed tasks, separately from the 320-task timing set. Incomplete action records affect 12 and eight tasks, respectively. Missing actions are excluded from both counts. Full generation has zero bypass by definition.

Measured time and deployment.

Task time spans the agent execution loop through terminal observation and result persistence. It includes decisions, browser operations, and observations, while excluding environment provisioning, browser teardown, and evaluator scoring. The measured mean for Full generation is 616.8 s on the matched task set.

Full generation uses temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.95, top-kk 40, high reasoning effort, and up to 16,384 output tokens. The hybrid runs combine temperature-zero attempts with temperature-one, top-pp-one length retries. Each replica occupies one GPU, with run-specific replica counts, concurrency, and browser placement. The reported task times characterize these evaluation deployments.

Appendix F Web Repair and Testing Protocol

F.1  Qualifying Browser Evidence

The main-text case in Figure 18 records browser testing and code repair during local-page development. To decide whether an observation justifies a product change, the proposed evaluation protocol first checks that the relevant test actions completed. A mismatch may otherwise originate in the test specification, the agent’s actions, or the environment (Yang et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2026).

Figure 35 uses a title-persistence requirement to make this decision concrete. Record R17 should retain Delivery plan v2 after reload. The Web Agent completes the edit and save, observes the new title, then reloads the record and finds the old title. Together, these observations support a candidate persistence defect. The report pairs the expected and observed values with the completed actions, tested build, reset state, and supporting artifacts, giving the Coding Agent a specific discrepancy to investigate.

The same old title has a different interpretation if Save could not be activated or reload did not complete. In that case, the test has not established that the product lost a saved value. The proposed adjudication rule therefore sends unresolved execution failures to diagnosis or bounded retesting. Test steps may be repaired and exploratory checks added while the issue’s acceptance goals and regression requirements stay fixed.

Repair feedback and final acceptance also serve different purposes. Feedback helps the agents revise a candidate. Final acceptance evaluates the submitted patch from a protected clean state, using checks the repair agents cannot change. Its verdict is withheld from further revision, so acceptance tests whether the fix survives beyond the session used to develop it.

Appendix I.4 details the common assignments, resets, and denominators needed to compare feedback conditions.

These controls support the proposed comparison of browser-feedback conditions (Wang et al., 2026b). Inclusion of an episode in model training follows the separate source and consumption accounting in Appendix D.

Appendix G NorthCUA Case Studies

The following cases trace complex software tasks from an initial workspace or source records to editable deliverables and native task outcomes. They illustrate sustained GUI interaction across geometry, data analysis, visual composition, circuit simulation, and gameplay. The GeoGebra, office, and TIDAL workflows use NorthCUA’s desktop MCP tools. The Virtuoso workflow uses native CUA Driver MCP tools in a prepared engineering environment. All use an external agent controller. The Zuma case extends this setting to screenshot-and-mouse gameplay. These demonstrations exercise the tool interface and are separate from the NorthCUA checkpoint evaluations in Section 6. The recorded step counts include GUI actions, observations, preparation, checks, and retries. The release packages preserve the full traces, infrastructure repairs, native outputs, and acceptance records.

G.1  Ruby Heart

The task is to turn supplied equations into a GeoGebra heart that can pulse, change depth and color, and reveal a moving cross-section. The difficulty is keeping the cutting plane and section linked to the changing surface. Figure 36 begins with an empty workspace. The agent enters native expressions to build a first construction, then arranges the geometry and four controls into an interactive exhibit. Construction view reveals the auxiliary geometry linked to the surface for inspection.

The agent then exercises these dependencies through playback and direct manipulation. Holding pulse phase and slice position fixed, it checks two depth settings that visibly change the surface and its section. It also reopens the saved file and later drags the slice to another position. The trace covers 18 combinations of depth, slice position, and pulse phase, connecting the visible shape to its underlying parameters. The 440-step record ends with the final saved .ggb and three separate view images. The editable construction supports continued interaction with the geometry established during modeling.

G.2  Silicon Atlas

This task asks for five editable plots from synthetic chip-test records. The challenge is preserving measurement meaning across spreadsheet analysis and plotting. Recorded failures take precedence. Otherwise, incomplete tests remain UNKNOWN, while missing current measurements stay missing. In Figure 37, the agent imports 2,142 sweep rows into Calc and fills formulas that classify 1,071 operating groups. A passing group requires two clean expected repeats, and energy is computed only for passing points. These rules govern the subsequent plots.

The classified table first feeds a Shmoo map of voltage and frequency in LabPlot. Matching axes on a second temperature map make the operating regions directly comparable. The agent next plots the maximum tested passing frequencies and passing-point energy. A separate 32-device sample supplies the final count plot, completing the atlas. The agent then reopens the workbook to check counts and units, repairs crowded labels, and exports the revised figure. The audit retains 573 passing, 489 failing, and nine unknown groups. After 928 recorded steps, the workbook and plotting project preserve the calculations and editable plots alongside the PDF and PNG outputs.

G.3  NOVA Presentation

The NOVA task asks for a six-slide presentation from a product brief, supplied images, and numerical data. The challenge is preserving accurate, editable scientific content while building a coherent visual story. Figure 38 starts with an empty presentation and a first cover. To support the performance slide, the agent computes mean signal-to-noise ratios from five repeats in Calc. The resulting table and supplied spectra feed native charts, which it embeds in Impress. Editable shapes and connectors then form the five-stage signal-path diagram.

The agent reads back the embedded chart data to check that application transfer preserved the calculation. The figure shows the same mean of 17.6268 at 5 ms in both views, making this check directly inspectable. A presentation-mode inspection covers all six slides before the 691-step record ends with an editable .odp, the calculation workbook, and a matching PDF. The task thus preserves a concrete numerical result through calculation, chart transfer, and final presentation. NOVA is a fictional product concept with illustrative imagery and numerical data.

G.4  CMOS Inverter Analysis

The task asks for a 1 V CMOS inverter, its DC transfer curve, and transistor operating-point checks in Virtuoso and Spectre. The difficulty is carrying the intended device and analysis settings from the schematic into the simulator, then connecting numerical readouts to the conditions that produced them. Figure 39 begins with an empty schematic. The agent sizes the two transistors, with the PMOS width and length fields shown in the figure. It then wires and labels the circuit and checks the completed design before configuring a 0–1 V input sweep with a 5 mV step. An uncommitted input edit then exposes a subtle GUI-state mismatch. The first sweep completes successfully, but the saved nominal input remains at 0 V. The agent returns to ADE, enters 0.5 V, commits it with Enter, and reruns the analysis so that the operating-point report uses the intended bias.

With the corrected configuration, the agent inspects the transfer curve in ViVA and locates the crossing of input and output near 0.498 V. This is an interpolated estimate from the 5 mV sweep. It separately reads both device reports at the nominal 0.5 V input, where the drain currents are +5.778​μ+5.778\,\muA and −5.778​μ-5.778\,\muA under the simulator’s sign convention. The 367-request record ends with the native schematic, simulator setup, waveform state, and operating-point evidence retained for inspection. The case shows how a sustained GUI workflow can carry a circuit through construction, configuration repair, and numerical interpretation while preserving the engineering artifacts behind the result. The supplied MOS1 models are constructed teaching models.

G.5  TIDAL-01 Modeling and Animation

TIDAL-01 asks for a silver-and-glass craft with a thin hull, swept inlays, and an opening iris beneath the body. The challenge is carrying this visual design from a two-dimensional drawing into editable geometry whose separate parts can be animated and inspected from different angles. Figure 40 begins with the top and side outlines in Inkscape, then shows the completed three-view sketch. The agent places this drawing beside a Blender blockout to match the thin side profile. It then shapes a swept curve on the hull and fits three inlays to its surface. To animate the underside opening, it assembles the iris from separately pivoted leaves and keys their opening poses. The close view of the eight-leaf assembly makes this change from static shape to articulated geometry visible.

An earlier render still shows pale, opaque inlays. The agent sets glass transmission to 1.0, then inspects a later render to assess transparency and contact with the hull. To refine the panel seats, it constructs three matching cutter volumes by extruding and rotating the inlay outlines. After further geometry work, an underside render exposes the optical ring and open iris. With these parts established, it keys a tracked camera arc that moves from the upper hull to the underside and returns to a rear-quarter view. The final strip combines whole-object views with glass and iris close-ups from the same editable scene, connecting the sketch’s silhouette and underside layout to the rendered object. Across 1,805 recorded steps, including observations, checks, and retries, the workflow produces an original SVG, a packed .blend, and a 12-second native animation with 288 frames at 24 fps. Reopening the packed scene reports no missing files. The case demonstrates a sustained 3D-authoring workflow in which geometric construction, material revision, and camera control contribute to one reusable animated asset.

G.6  Zuma Gameplay

Turns and tunnels change the accessible targets in this six-color Jaguar-level task. Figure 41 begins with a purple match and progresses to a six-shot chain bonus. At 5,020 points, the progress bar turns green with balls still in play. The agent swaps blue ammunition for green, clears the exposed pair, and works through the bend to a short bottom-lane tail. It eliminates the last purple and red groups, waits for the completion bonus, and reaches native STATS with 9,070 points after 199 GUI actions.

Appendix H Runtime and Admission Protocols

This appendix defines the runtime choices needed to interpret an interaction record, including the observations presented to the policy, the tools available to each role, environment ownership, and demonstration selection. The learning-side segment and update rules are consolidated in Appendix E.5.

H.1  Runtime Configuration

A context profile determines which retained interactions enter each model call. The sliding visual profile counts the latest clean frame within its image budget and keeps textual action/result records after image eviction. Other profiles replay visual history within a compaction epoch. Text windows, image budgets, and semantic compaction are separate settings. The generic context manager defaults to off. Shadow mode records decisions without applying them, and enforce mode applies its configured policy.

Historical overlays mark issued actions on pre-action images, while the latest clean frame shows the currently observed state. Text-only tools, including notes, do not add visual frames. A later application change can require waiting or a fresh observation. After a timeout or failed refresh, state inspection precedes retry. Web element references belong to the observed page state, and failed refreshes invalidate affected aliases.

Compaction retains a structured account of the goal, constraints, supported facts, completed work, failures, current state, open items, and artifact references. Summaries and notes carry their temporal provenance and remain distinguishable from observations. The summary prompt, protected recent interactions, trigger/target budgets, and failure policy determine the resulting input. Note categories are fact, correction, precaution, constraint, decision, and checkpoint. Compatibility names map mistake to correction and plan/other to checkpoint. The exposed schema, replacement behavior, and prompt budget control which notes remain visible.

Execution scopes and tool interfaces.

A session binds the agent to its environment and resources. A round tracks one request and execution budget, and a step records one policy-decision and action-execution iteration. A step can contain several tool calls, so model decisions, tool calls, and GUI interactions are different counts. The dispatcher validates declared arguments before invoking local handlers or connected MCP tools and returns results to the requesting step. Appendix H.2 specifies the model-facing interfaces. Runtime probes use a separate permission profile from actor tools.

Evaluator profiles and attribution.

Evaluation binds a task and rubric to an evidence source, inspection permissions, budget, and report schema. The rubric-generation template requests three to seven criteria. The Agent Kit desktop entry path can use a request-level fallback, while the web profile supplies eight fixed criteria. The selected profile determines which criteria, weights, applicability rules, and reward conversion apply. Report-format validation checks the report’s structure.

Artifact tools inspect retained records. Live tools additionally require authorization and a dispatcher bound to the evaluated workspace. Artifact-only replay has no live device access. Read-only probes are preferred. Shell inspection uses an allowlist, and state-changing GUI or browser inspection requires explicit permission. The workspace remains reserved through required live checks.

Actor credit depends on the state before evaluator intervention. Terminal evidence and evaluator actions are therefore recorded separately. Inspection checks the submitted artifact or page state. A potentially mutating check needs a procedure that preserves the original state, such as a prepared evaluation copy. When that basis cannot be preserved, assessment uses retained evidence or leaves the condition unresolved. Probe failure, conflicting evidence, and an exhausted inspection budget are distinct from a supported task-failure verdict. When evaluator protection is enabled, recognized evaluation failures remain unresolved without replacing the actor’s terminal status.

H.2  Action Spaces and Parameter Schemas

The desktop and web instances in Section 3.1.3 expose different tools through the same dispatcher. The tables below summarize their model-facing contracts and the evaluator interfaces in Section 3.3. Fields with neither a default nor a question mark are required. A question mark marks an optional field with no supplied value, and T[] denotes an array. Empty arguments are written as {}. These are tool signatures, independent of provider-specific call envelopes. Runtime-only probes and environment-setup commands are outside the acting agents’ action spaces.

H.2.1  Desktop Agent

Desktop actions address the current screen and focused application. Coordinates follow the run’s declared coordinate policy, which maps the model’s image coordinates to device coordinates. A drag point has the schema {x: number, y: number}. The button argument accepts left, right, or middle.

The note categories are fact, mistake, precaution, plan, constraint, decision, and other. These exposed names map to the working-memory categories described in Appendix H.1. The same note fields apply to web_note below.

H.2.2  Web Agent

Web actions can use element references from the latest page observation or viewport-relative CSS coordinates. In Table 22, Ref is a string or integer element label. References are refreshed with page state, while tab_ref identifies a browser tab. Point actions use nonnegative CSS coordinates measured from the current viewport’s top-left corner. These differ from full-page or resized-image coordinates.

H.2.3  Evaluator

The evaluator retrieves recorded evidence and, when authorized, inspects the evaluated workspace through live tools. Table 23 separates these interfaces. The active desktop or web profile selects the applicable tools. Evidence references identify saved artifacts, independently of the web agent’s element references. Retrieval tools with detail_level use standard by default and accept debug for expanded records.

Authorized desktop GUI inspection reuses the schemas in Table 21 through client_gui_screenshot, client_gui_click, client_gui_type, client_gui_keypress, and client_gui_wait. Additional browser operations use the matching client_browser_ wrappers and schemas from Table 22, excluding web_note. State-changing inspection requires explicit permission and follows the attribution protocol in Appendix H.1.

Evaluation ends with final_report, whose required fields appear in Table 24. Optional structured fields carry criterion scores, diagnoses, side effects, safety and efficiency assessments, and evidence-linked divergence information. The web report additionally records the final URL and title, verification flags, a blocker category, and critical evidence references.

H.3  Batch Collection and Resource Ownership

Task preparation binds CaseSpec to its inputs, initialization procedure, application/tool profile, budgets, and optional post-run checks. Placement considers configured evaluator requirements as well as actor requirements. Resumed work uses the original task and configuration identity. Supported context-managed settings are retained in batch-local snapshots, while external dependencies keep their own version records.

Fresh single-use sandboxes isolate new collection attempts. Task-specific fixtures also cover external accounts and service state. An optional prepared queue, disabled by library default, performs initialization ahead of execution. Reservations are task/attempt-specific and assigned once. On-demand acquisition is a separate fallback. Prepared queues and warm pools have different allocation and reuse rules. An externally owned environment retains its own termination authority.

Creation, preparation, execution, submission, and status-query limits govern different resources. Assignment checks the remaining provider lifetime against the task timeout and release margin. Attempt identifiers link scheduler state to controller state, and reconciliation checks an existing attempt before starting another. A scheduler claim and a device execution lease represent distinct ownership decisions.

Live evaluation and environment-resident output capture finish before owned resources are released. Once a sandbox is destroyed, replay is limited to retained artifacts. Unconfirmed cleanup remains unresolved and continues to incur resource cost until destruction is confirmed. This lifecycle distinguishes transport disconnection from environment termination.

H.4  Cohort Admission

Outcome-verified completion demonstrations require actor-only extraction, valid action/context alignment, required artifacts, full-task acceptance, and the cohort’s quality checks. Broad judge-filtered mid-training uses its separately declared selector, and evaluator demonstrations are separate judgment-task samples (Appendix E.1). Online RL retains valid negative outcomes within task groups.

Appendix I Benchmark Evaluation Details

Section 6.1 introduces the six benchmarks. This appendix collects the metric definitions, task sets, and implementation settings used to interpret the results, together with the sources of published baseline scores.

Comparable tasks and interfaces.

Interactive evaluation uses the benchmark’s scorer independently of the harness evaluator used for collection. OSWorld-Verified uses the supported 361-task setting without the eight Google Drive tasks. Our OSWorld 2.0 binary-completion and partial scores both use the full 108-task set. Grounding records identify the OSWorld-G instruction variant and absent-target convention, and map crop/resize predictions back to annotation coordinates.

WebArena-Verified retains the responses and network traces required by its scorer. Our WebTestBench evaluation supplies the gold checklist directly, following the benchmark’s oracle setting. Agents return Pass/Fail judgments, with Fail as the positive class. Precision, recall, and F1 measure defect detection. The gold checklist fixes the inspection scope for defect detection. We first compute precision, recall, and F1 from the checklist judgments within each task, then average each metric over all evaluated tasks. For task-level scores Pt,Rt,F1,t∈[0,1]P_{t},R_{t},F_{1,t}\in[0,1] across NN tasks, the reported percentages are

P¯=100N​∑t=1NPt,R¯=100N​∑t=1NRt,F¯1=100N​∑t=1NF1,t.\overline{P}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}P_{t},\qquad\overline{R}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}R_{t},\qquad\overline{F}_{1}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}F_{1,t}. (6)

This task-level macro average gives equal weight to tasks with different checklist lengths. It differs from pooling all checklist judgments into one confusion matrix. In particular, F¯1\overline{F}_{1} averages the per-task F1 scores and generally differs from the harmonic mean of P¯\overline{P} and R¯\overline{R}. Table 11 reports all three metrics for each included model and omits models without measured results. The NorthCUA Nano, Mini, and Pro results all use final checkpoints after joint desktop–web RL.

The source notes below record the task scope, tool permissions, budgets, and scoring conventions of published baselines. Parameter columns distinguish total from activated language-model counts. Within each NorthCUA tier, stage comparisons use the declared benchmark tasks, tools, observations, and execution budgets.

Repeated predictions.

Table 29 summarizes repeated predictions on the same grounding examples, including run-to-run variation and pass@3 (Dror et al., 2018). The accompanying task-level breakdowns explain coverage and execution behavior. Showcase demonstrations are described separately from model checkpoint evaluation.

I.1  Grounding Scores and Repeated Sampling

The direct SSP evaluation produces one coordinate prediction from a full screenshot. Table 27 breaks down the final-model evaluation records by application group and target type. Every domain uses the same sample set for Nano, Mini, and Pro. This makes the coverage differences visible without changing the task distribution between models.

We further stratify SSP by target size and type (Table 28). Target size is the smaller of the annotated box’s width and height, min⁡(x2−x1,y2−y1)\min(x_{2}-x_{1},y_{2}-y_{1}) in the original image coordinates. Fixed boundaries at 16 and 32 pixels define the three exploratory size bins. Predictions are paired across all three models by the exact image filename and query. All 1,581 identities are unique and matched, with identical reference boxes and target-type labels. The bins measure geometric extent in the original screenshot before model preprocessing.

The paired Nano–Mini predictions show 1,086 items correct for both models, 375 correct only for Mini, 66 correct only for Nano, and 54 missed by both. Mini locates 375 of Nano’s 429 misses, but each model also has unique successes. For Mini and Pro, 1,373 items are correct for both, 102 only for Pro, 88 only for Mini, and 18 for neither. Pro’s net gain of 14 correct items therefore coexists with distinct successes from each model. The paired counts distinguish shared errors from checkpoint-specific successes.

Pro’s remaining 106 errors all produce valid coordinates outside the target box. Icons account for 59 errors, including 46 in the 16–<32<32 pixel band. That band contains 418 icon targets, of which 11.0% are missed, and contributes 43.4% of Pro’s errors overall. On icons smaller than 16 pixels, Pro reaches 93.0% accuracy. Across application groups, Pro gains most over Mini in CAD (3.1 points) and scientific software (2.4 points), while development software is 1.0 point lower.

OSWorld-G Refined uses temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.95, top-kk 40, and a 1,024-token output limit. Table 29 reports the mean and sample standard deviation over three complete runs, alongside the best complete-run accuracy used in the main comparison. Pass@3 counts an item as correct when at least one of its three predictions succeeds.

On SSP, Pro raises single-run accuracy by 0.9 percentage points over Mini and reaches 95.6% pass@3, 2.3 points above its single-run result.

The Refined records contain 564 unique item IDs in each run, with matched annotations across all three models and all three draws. Of these, 510 have visible targets, comprising 470 rectangular and 40 polygonal reference regions. The other 54 require an absent-target refusal. Visible-target accuracy uses the corresponding region test, and refusal accuracy uses the benchmark’s designated no-target output.

All three tiers share the grounding system prompt, sampling settings, and coordinate scoring. Nano and Mini use a grounding-specific click schema that describes normalized coordinates and refusal, requires x, y, and button, and enumerates button choices. Pro uses the frozen NorthCUA desktop click schema, whose descriptions refer to desktop interaction and whose button argument is optional. The reported tier differences therefore describe these evaluated model and interface configurations.

Table 30 reports how often each item succeeds. Nano’s three complete runs contain 467, 460, and 468 correct predictions, while Mini’s contain 488, 496, and 492, and Pro’s contain 504, 509, and 513. All runs have zero request errors and unparsed predictions. Pro’s second run includes one separately completed missing item, yielding the same 564 unique IDs as the other runs. This completion contributes one prediction for that item to run 2 and adds no extra draw to pass@3.

Pro’s 34 persistently missed items contribute 102 of its 166 incorrect predictions (61.5%). Its remaining 41 items vary across draws, while 489 succeed in all three. Mini and Pro share 17 persistent misses, and 16 items remain persistently incorrect across all three model tiers. These counts show that Pro reduces the recurring error set while leaving a smaller common subset unresolved. The 1,692 predictions are repeated measurements of 564 items across 251 screenshots.

The improvement also spans reference geometries (Table 31). On rectangular targets, Pro averages 91.1%, compared with Mini’s 87.9%. Polygonal regions are already high-performing for Mini at 97.5%, and Pro reaches 98.3%. The geometry labels identify the benchmark’s scoring regions, not separate semantic task categories. Together with the absent-target analysis in the main text, they identify refusal decisions as a larger remaining gap than polygonal targeting.

I.2  Interactive Results and Trajectory Breakdowns

The main WebArena-Verified table reports final RL checkpoints at 67.2% for Nano, 70.4% for Mini, and 73.9% for Pro. Pro’s score comes from one complete evaluation of all 812 tasks. The trajectory breakdowns below cover Nano and Mini after SFT and Pro after RL, with 521, 552, and 600 successful tasks, respectively. Mini uses the second evaluation round, matching Figure 27.

The earlier SFT evaluations additionally report pass@3 of 69.3% for Nano and 73.9% for Mini. Figure 27 includes Mini’s SFT website-level breakdown alongside Nano SFT and Pro RL.

Table 32 groups the 812 tasks by website scope and requested outcome. Website groups use the task’s site set, pooling multi-site combinations into one group. Outcome types follow the evaluator’s expected category. Each grouping therefore partitions the same task set and reveals a different aspect of task completion.

Mini’s additional completions over Nano concentrate in state-changing and retrieval tasks, with 13 and 19 more successes, respectively, while their navigation counts are nearly identical. Pro reaches 75.4% on retrieval, 73.3% on state change, and 71.7% on navigation. Cross-site work is more demanding for all three checkpoints, with 7, 12, and 17 successes out of 48 tasks. In comparison, Pro completes 76.3% of the 764 single-site tasks.

Mini’s records show how this difference relates to execution length within one checkpoint. It completes 540 of 764 single-site tasks (70.7%) and 12 of 48 cross-site tasks (25.0%). Their median lengths are 10 and 27.5 decisions, respectively. Even among successful tasks, the cross-site median is 17 decisions, compared with nine for single-site work. These tasks combine lower completion with longer interactions, making them a useful focus for experience that trains the agent to carry constraints and intermediate results between websites.

Table 33 summarizes decision counts by evaluator outcome. Each record contributes its current assistant response once, including the final response. Nano has 811 traced tasks and one untraced failure, while Mini and Pro each have 812. All 812 tasks enter each model’s success-rate denominator. Quartiles use linear interpolation at (n−1)​p(n-1)p for percentile fraction pp.

Successful tasks have similar median lengths of 9, 10, and 10 decisions for Nano, Mini, and Pro. Failed tasks have longer medians of 19, 18, and 15.5 decisions and contribute 58.5%, 50.6%, and 38.4% of their recorded decisions, respectively. For Mini, this is 7,698 of 15,224 decisions across 260 failures. Separating outcomes thus exposes the disproportionate execution devoted to unsuccessful tasks. At the same time, Pro completes 24 tasks with at least 50 decisions, including a 93-decision success, showing that extended execution can also support successful completion.

Mini likewise completes 13 tasks with at least 50 decisions, with its longest success taking 75. Across all three checkpoints, successful-task means exceed their medians, reflecting a tail of extended but productive execution. This profile favors training examples that retain successful long trajectories alongside concise workflows. In our learning pipeline, outcome-based selection retains successful long workflows for supervision, while RL also uses unsuccessful attempts to provide negative feedback.

The browser case in Figure 31 is task 1 in the Pro export. Its 13 decisions include an unavailable-option error, inspection of the actual dropdown choices, and successful completion after revising the report settings. The screenshots show how inspecting the available choices resolves the error and lets the agent finish the report query.

The desktop checkpoint summaries cover 361 OSWorld-Verified tasks with a 100-step limit and the full 108-task OSWorld 2.0 set with a 500-step limit. The OSWorld-Verified main table uses the RL checkpoints at 78.9%, 85.3%, and 88.6% for Nano, Mini, and Pro. Tables 12 and 13 retain the earlier checkpoints for stage comparisons. On OSWorld 2.0, the final RL checkpoints have Binary/Partial scores of 13.0/45.6 for Nano, 18.5/50.1 for Mini, and 30.6/66.8 for Pro. The Mid pairs are 0.9/24.2, 2.8/25.6, and 9.3/30.6, respectively. The long-horizon SFT checkpoints score 12.0/40.9, 18.5/46.3, and 27.3/63.6 in the same tier order. These SFT checkpoints serve as the Before-RL baselines in Table 13. The binary and partial scores describe full completion and intermediate progress on the same tasks.
